Its name, Yoshuji, nods to Yoshu, an old poetic name for the region around Kyoto. Where Japanese shojin ryori tends toward austerity, fucha ryori is a little warmer and more generous, drawing on vegetable oil and bolder seasoning, which makes it approachable even for first-timers. The setting is intimate and quiet, with tatami rooms that feel more like dining in a private temple residence than a restaurant. · Cooking that lets the natural flavor of seasonal vegetables come forward, in the Zen Buddhist spirit of simple, mindful, meat-free dining. · Seasonal plant-based courses in the fucha ryori tradition. places.n: 餃子屋もり (Gyoza-ya Mori)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — two ladies, best gyoza in the area] Run by two women who cook right in front of you in a tiny, cosy bar-restaurant. Pork & cabbage gyoza, rice omelette, drinks. One reviewer said: 'without a doubt, these were the best gyoza I've ever had.' Another: 'our favourite small bar/restaurant of the trip.' Address: Nishinokyo Enmachi 21-2, north of Enmachi station. Evenings only. Cash expected.
places.chef: proprietress / okami-san (owner-operator) · Nishinokyo-Encho, Nakagyo Ward, Kyoto (a short walk north of Enmachi) · A tiny, counter-only neighborhood gyoza spot run by its proprietress (the okami-san), who gives the place a warm, homey feel that regulars single out. Despite the name, it works as much like a friendly local izakaya as a dumpling shop, and it is the kind of small counter where you can comfortably come alone, settle in, and stay a while. · Handmade gyoza. The grilled 'bari-bari' gyoza are the signature: a crisp, thick wrapper packed with plenty of meaty filling, served with a miso-based dipping sauce or vinegar and soy. Chewy water gyoza (sui-gyoza) are the other house favorite. The menu stretches well beyond dumplings into izakaya fare, including fried dishes such as karaage.

places.n: 焼鳥 雷 本店 (Yakitori Kaminari – Honten)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — 15-seat yakitori counter] Run by two people: the yakitori master and one assistant. 8 counter seats facing the grill, 2 small tables — 15 total. English menu available. Reviewers call it 'common man yakitori, not pretentious, authentic local dining experience.' Try the chicken tail (shiri). No reservation needed. Evenings only. Note: may be the 雷 Enmachi location or a nearby branch — confirm address with Google Maps.
places.chef: owner, grill master · Mibu / Shijō-Ōmiya, Kyoto · This is the original (honten) location of a small, much-loved neighborhood yakitori shop in the Mibu area near Shijō-Ōmiya, open since 1994. It has the unpretentious look and easygoing feel of a classic street-corner yakitori joint, and over the years it has built a devoted following for honest charcoal grilling at down-to-earth prices. The kitchen runs as a true one-man operation: a single master mans the charcoal, doing the prep and the grilling himself, and regulars love watching him work the skewers with quick, practiced hands right in front of them. · Authentic charcoal yakitori done simply and well, at prices that keep it a genuine everyday neighborhood spot. · Charcoal-grilled chicken cooked over a strong, close flame. The hatsu (chicken heart) is the standout that reviewers single out again and again, alongside excellent liver (kimo) and a fresh, moist chicken tataki. There are playful skewers too, like asparagus wrapped with chicken and topped with mayonnaise and crushed nuts, and pork belly with tomato and cheese. Skewers come in both tare (sauce) and shio (salt) preparations.
places.gfd: Standard yakitori tare sauce contains soy sauce (wheat). Ask about salt-grilled (shio) options which avoid tare. Not confirmed GF-safe.
places.vgd: Yakitori is skewered grilled chicken. Not suitable for vegans.

places.n: 京料理 万長 (Kyoto Cuisine Mancho)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — traditional Kyoto cuisine near Myoshinji] Tsurezure bento lunch sets, traditional Kyoto tableware, koto music, spotless and peaceful. 107 reviews mostly in Japanese. English menu available. 'A true culinary experience' — one visitor. 24 Taniguchisonomachi, Ukyo Ward (northwest Kyoto, near Myoshinji temple complex). Lunch only on weekdays; lunch and dinner weekends.
places.chef: Akio Ishitani · owner, chef · Myoshinji / Ukyo Ward, Kyoto · Manchō has been serving Kyoto cuisine for around 80 years, founded around 1940 and now run by the Ishitani family, with Akio Ishitani (石谷彰男) at the helm. It sits in the quiet temple district of northwest Kyoto, directly across from the north gate of Myoshinji, the great head temple of the Rinzai Zen school, and within walking distance of Ninna-ji and Ryoan-ji along the Kinukake-no-Michi. It is a neighborhood institution that locals have known for generations, the kind of place a family returns to across decades for celebrations, memorial gatherings, and seasonal lunches. · The restaurant's guiding idea is to create the flavors of Kyoto with the heart (京の味を心で創る), valuing connections and heartfelt hospitality with the people it serves. · The house signature is the Tsuredure Bento (つれづれ弁当), a seasonal Kyoto bento whose dishes change with the four seasons. Beyond the bento, Manchō is known for Edo-style grilled eel hitsumabushi and eel kaiseki, and for spring specialties built around Kyoto bamboo shoots, with tempura of seasonal vegetables such as bamboo shoot and rape blossom that diners single out as crisp and delicious.
places.gfd: Traditional Kyoto set meals (bento). Soy sauce (wheat) used throughout. Some dishes may be wheat-light but no GF guarantee.
places.vgd: Kyoto cuisine often features tofu, yuba, and vegetables alongside fish. Ask about vegetarian options in the bento sets.

places.n: キコク食堂 (Kikoku Shokudō)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — Shōwa-era kushiage counter since 1949] A tiny evening-only spot across from the Umeyu bathhouse: 12 counter seats plus two small tables (20 total). places.chef: Father / front-of-house and drinks, Mother / kitchen and cooking · Shimogyō, Kyoto · A wonderfully lived-in neighborhood eatery tucked along the Takase River just by Gojō, directly across from the much-loved Umeyu sentō. Though the sign says "shokudō," it really comes alive only in the evening, more tavern than canteen, with red lanterns out front and a worn, comfortable room where you can settle in and lose track of time. It is run as a true mom-and-pop spot by an older couple: the father works the front, pouring drinks and chatting with guests, while the mother runs the kitchen and is known for her warm, homestyle cooking and famously generous portions. Cutlets are coated in fine breadcrumbs and fried right in front of you at the counter, coming out crisp and reasonably priced. Many people stumble in for the first time after a soak at the Umeyu bathhouse across the street. · Hand-breaded kushiage / kushikatsu skewers (around 70 yen a stick), fried fresh at the counter, alongside homey izakaya plates like generously piled potato salad, dote-yaki, ham and eggs, and a demi-glace hamburger.

places.n: みやこ食堂 (Miyako Shokudō)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — neighbourhood udon diner] An old-style local shokudō near Tamba-guchi/Umekōji with 28 seats, open all day, budget prices (under ¥1,000). Udon, donburi and side dishes from a display case. No English. Carry cash. Reviews are overwhelmingly Japanese (assessed from Tabelog presence / negligible English footprint — not a counted ratio).
places.chef: owner · Kyoto, Japan · Miyako Shokudo is a homespun neighborhood diner tucked into the old Shimahara shopping arcade, a short walk from Tanbaguchi Station in the quiet streets near Nishi Hongan-ji. It is the kind of small, family-run shokudo that has all but disappeared from modern Kyoto: walls papered top to bottom with handwritten menu strips, a glass display case of ready-made sides, and plain tables shared by neighbors. Diners describe stepping inside as feeling like a trip back to childhood, eating the simple, traditional flavors of an older Kyoto. The owner runs the room personally and is remembered as warm and welcoming, and the whole place carries the unpretentious, lived-in character of a true local canteen. · Comforting udon and budget-friendly set meals are the heart of the menu. Regulars come for the keiran (egg) udon and ankake (thick, glossy gravy) udon, alongside donburi like oyakodon, and homestyle teishoku such as the kashiwa mizutaki (chicken hot-pot) set and tonkatsu set. The hand-cut kamaboko fish cake in the noodle bowls is singled out as a small but memorable touch, and a case of inari sushi, rolled sushi, and karaage rounds out the offerings.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop — market canteen, 50+ years] A 16-seat self-service diner INSIDE the Kyoto Central Wholesale Market, feeding market workers and early risers from 4am. Pick sides from the display, pay, eat. This is a working market — go early, be unobtrusive, and check the market’s closure calendar before making a trip. No English. Cash. Reviews are overwhelmingly Japanese (assessed from Tabelog presence / negligible English footprint — not a counted ratio).
places.chef: Murakami Tadaaki · owner, chef · Kyoto · Murakami Shokudo is a Showa-era market canteen that has fed Kyoto's Central Wholesale Market neighborhood for more than half a century. The kitchen has passed from the founder to the current second-generation owner, Murakami Tadaaki, who keeps the same homey, comforting flavors handed down from the previous generation. Ingredients are bought fresh each day from the wholesale market right outside the door, and the dining room still has its nostalgic retro feel, with table seating and a tatami area in back. It opens before dawn to feed market workers, taxi drivers, and locals alike. · Honest, home-cooked taste at market prices, served from before dawn so the people who run the market always have a warm meal waiting.

places.n: 淡海食堂 (Awumi Shokudō)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — tiny old neighbourhood diner] A hushed, time-worn soba/udon shokudō in a residential pocket near Shōkoku-ji, signature dish katsudon, budget prices, cash only. Local write-ups describe it as roughly a century old and now third-generation (not independently confirmed). Closed Tue and the 2nd/3rd Wed; hours approximate — call ahead (075-211-0617). places.chef: owner · Kamigyo, Kyoto (near Shokoku-ji / Kuramaguchi) · Tucked into a quiet residential street in Kamigyo, a short walk from Shokoku-ji and Kuramaguchi, Awumi Shokudo is a neighborhood diner with roughly a century of history behind it. Stepping inside feels like a trip back to the Showa era - the room is genuinely old but kept clean and tidy, full of the unpretentious, nostalgic atmosphere that long-running local eateries are loved for. It is the kind of homey, affordable place that has quietly fed its neighborhood for generations. · The house signature is the katsudon: a single pork cutlet, cut and bound together with a firm-set egg, served over rice with takuan pickles on the side and finished with a fragrant lift of sansho pepper. The pork is tender and the batter soaks up the broth so the dashi, egg, and cutlet come together in every bite. Beyond that they keep an old-school shokudo lineup of udon, soba, rice bowls, and set meals.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop — family eel house, 12 seats] A small lunch-only unagi specialist near Nishiki, opened in 2018 by the family behind 大國屋, a Nishiki Market river-fish/eel shop founded in 1912. Charcoal jiyaki-grilled eel with clay-pot rice; reservations recommended; ¥6,000–8,000. Pricier and more special-occasion than a humble diner, but family-run and tiny. places.chef: owner-family, eel specialist (unagi) · Kyoto, Japan · Ōkuniya is a river-fish and eel specialist with deep roots in Kyoto's Nishiki Market, where the family shop has traded for generations (the market lists the house as founded in 1912 and now run by its fourth-generation owner). The shop sells charcoal-grilled eel, 'bubu unagi' (eel with Japanese pepper and tare), eel yawata-maki, and tsukudani-style river fish, keeping live fish in tanks at the back and preparing to order. In 2018 the family opened a small sit-down restaurant, Manbei, on Sakaimachi-dōri just above Nishiki-kōji, next door to the Michelin-starred Naru-ya. It is an intimate room of about a dozen seats with no printed menu. · A pursuit of simple deliciousness — the best eel and the best rice, and little else. Everything is timed to the meal: rice started when you arrive, eel grilled to order over charcoal, the crackle and aroma of the binchōtan treated as part of the experience. · One thing, done completely: jiyaki unagi with okudo-san clay-pot rice. Domestic eel (notably from Mikawa-Isshiki in Aichi, with rare wild eel from the Seto Inland Sea in season) is prepared Kansai-style — split from the belly, head on, gri…

places.chef: owner-operated · Shijo-Muromachi, Shimogyo Ward, Kyoto · Manpuku is a beloved old-school eatery tucked into the corner of Shijo-Muromachi in central Kyoto, where it has been serving its neighborhood for over 80 years. Step inside and you feel time slow down: the small, roughly 20-seat room has kept the same nostalgic, mid-century Showa-era atmosphere it had at its founding, right down to the television flickering in the corner. It is the kind of unpretentious working-class shokudo that locals have grown up with, the sort of place that, as one writer put it, 'blends in too much' with the busy street outside. Generations of Kyoto diners describe its bowl as the very taste of their childhood. · The house signature is chuka soba, a classic Showa-style Chinese noodle soup. The broth is a light, gentle shoyu (soy) base carried by subtle Japanese dashi, paired with medium-thin noodles. Regulars often order it as a set with a kitsune-don (fried-tofu rice bowl), and braised beef tendon is another fondly mentioned offering.

places.chef: family-run shokudo, katsudon and udon specialist · Kyoto, Japan · Matsunoya has stood in the back streets near Karasuma-Imadegawa, just behind Doshisha University's Imadegawa campus, since 1940. It has been a family-run neighborhood shokudo for over 80 years, and the present generation traces back to the owner's mother, who married into the family in 1963 and has helped run the kitchen ever since. What began as a humble udon shop grew into a Kyoto institution thanks to the hungry students next door: in the 1960s, Doshisha students kept asking for 'more food, make the portions bigger,' and the family obliged. The oversized katsudon born from those requests has stayed at roughly the same generous size for more than half a century, and the shop has fed generations of Doshisha students, locals, and longtime regulars ever since. · Hold onto tradition while never standing still: the kitchen keeps the portions at their original 1960s scale and the seasoning bold enough to carry a mountain of rice, while the current owner keeps developing new dishes to keep regulars coming back. · The signature dish is the katsudon: a thick, crisply fried wheat-breaded pork cutlet bound with fluffy half-s…

places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto · Kikō is a long-running, family-run tofu and kappō counter tucked along Kiyamachi, near the Kamogawa River. The shop is around 70 years old and is run by a proprietress (the okami) who took it over from her father. Its roots run deep into Kyoto's tofu culture: the family's main business is a neighboring tofu maker, so the tofu served here comes straight from that lineage. The restaurant began life serving yudofu (simmered hot tofu) as its centerpiece, and tofu remains at the heart of the experience. What truly sets the place apart is the river: the family has long held the rare privilege of fishing the Kamogawa, a tradition the father carried on as a licensed fisherman and the current owner continues herself, bringing river fish straight to the counter. · Seasonal Kyoto cooking meant to be enjoyed unhurried, paired with a drink — honest, carefully prepared small dishes rather than abundance, rooted in the family's own tofu and fish from the river running past the door. · Beautifully simple Kyoto tofu — above all yudofu (hot simmered tofu) made with tofu from the family's own tofu shop — served alongside seasonal river fish caught in the Kamogawa, such as morok…

places.chef: Miyamoto Hisami · owner · Nishijin (Senbon-Imadegawa), Kamigyo Ward, Kyoto · Shizuka opened in 1937 in the heart of the old Nishijin weaving district, and it carries an unusual origin: the name comes from a Pontocho geiko named Shizuka, whose former residence became the cafe. The year after it opened, Miyamoto Ryoichi — the grandfather of the present proprietor's husband — took over the business, and it has stayed in the Miyamoto family ever since, now run by the third generation. It's regarded as one of the oldest coffee houses in the neighborhood. Walk in and you step straight into the Showa era: white plaster walls, candy-colored wooden furniture, velvet-upholstered seats designed to evoke a train carriage, and rows of vintage coffee mills the founders collected over the decades. A 2016 renovation was done carefully so the original 1937 character was kept intact. The shop has long been a quiet refuge for the area's geiko and maiko, who would slip in for a cup of coffee. · Everything on the menu is made from scratch in-house, and the family has chosen to preserve the cafe's original 1937 feel rather than modernize it, so guests can slow down and spend unhurried time in a room th…

places.chef: owner, soba craftsman · 北山 (Kitayama), Sakyo-ku, Kyoto · Kitayama-Gonbe is a small, family-run soba house tucked along Kyoto's Kitayama street, a short walk from Kitayama Station. It has quietly kept to the same craft for years: the owner hand-cuts soba on the premises every day, working in a deliberately small kitchen. The shop has a homely two-floor layout, with table seating downstairs and a quieter tatami room upstairs, and it leans into the rhythm of the seasons with a menu that changes month to month. · A small shop that, in the owner's own words, makes its soba with care every single day. The emphasis is on doing a few things well: hand-cut noodles, a from-scratch multi-stage dashi (first, second and third extractions), and seasonal dishes that rotate through the year. · Handmade ni-hachi soba, cut to a roughly 80% buckwheat / 20% wheat ratio (the proportion shifts a little with the season), served cold as seiro/zaru or in a hot dashi broth. The kitchen is known for a clean, honest multi-stage dashi, so the simplest bowls let the broth speak for itself. Tempura is a highlight too, including a kamaage and a tenzaru featuring two live tiger prawns fried to order.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. Soba noodles here are not certified 100% buckwheat (typical soba contains wheat flour binder), tempura/donburi use wheat, and the soy-based dashi/tsuyu contains wheat. places.chef: owner, chef · 京都駅周辺 (near Kyoto Station), Shimogyo Ward, Kyoto · Yamamoto Manbo is one of the founding homes of Kyoto-style okonomiyaki, run by the same family for three generations since around 1950. It was opened by founder Yamamoto Yukie; the business then passed to her younger brother as the second generation, and today it is her nephew, the third generation, who keeps the curtain hanging over the door. Tucked into municipal housing a short walk east of Kyoto Station, it is a true neighborhood institution, the kind of counter spot regulars and curious travelers crowd around to watch the big iron griddle at work. Locals will tell you that you cannot really talk about Kyoto okonomiyaki without mentioning this shop, often credited as a birthplace of the city's distinctive griddle styles. · The house signature is manbo-yaki, a Kyoto-original okonomiyaki that is neither Osaka-style nor Hiroshima-style. A thin wheat-flour batter is layered with ingredients like beef tendon (suji), oil cracklings (abura-kasu), squid, offal (horumon), green onion and takuan pickles, then combined with griddle-fried noodles and finished with egg. Diners get to customize it three ways: noodles (udon or …

places.chef: soba maker, owner · Kitano Hakubaicho, Kyoto · Soba Shubou Ichii opened on December 14, 2015, in a renovated traditional Kyoto machiya townhouse tucked into the quiet streets near Kinkaku-ji and Ryoan-ji, about ten minutes on foot from Kitano Hakubaicho (and a minute from Waratenjin). It is a soba-focused izakaya where the noodles are taken seriously: only the amount of buckwheat needed for that day is ground fresh on a stone mill, and the technique is adjusted each day to the condition of the flour. The kitchen draws soft spring water from Kyomitoge in the Kyoto hills for both the dough and the dashi, the idea being to let the natural fragrance and flavor of the buckwheat and the broth come through cleanly. · A craft-first approach summed up by the kitchen's own words about grinding small and grinding daily so they can 'have a conversation with the buckwheat flour' and coax out the best possible soba, paired with careful sourcing of water and ingredients. · Hand-cut, stone-ground soba offered at different buckwheat ratios, including a nihachi (roughly 80% buckwheat, 20% wheat), a nine-tenths blend, and a juwari (100% buckwheat). places.chef: owner, chef · 左京区 浄土寺 — along the Philosopher's Path (哲学の道), near Ginkaku-ji, Kyoto · Jugo (十五) is a tiny made-to-order soba shop that opened in 2017, tucked along the Philosopher's Path near Ginkaku-ji. It seats only six or seven at a counter and is run single-handedly by its owner, who polishes and mills his own buckwheat in advance, then hand-rolls, cuts, and boils each order in front of you at the counter milling-and-rolling station. The name 十五 ("fifteen") nods to the shop's signature commitment to freshness: rather than the traditional three-fresh (三たて) ideal, the owner practices a five-fresh (五立て) approach — polished-fresh, ground-fresh, hand-rolled-fresh, cut-fresh, and boiled-fresh. places.chef: owner, soba chef · Murasakino, Kyoto · Kanei sits inside a roughly 100-year-old Kyoto machiya in the quiet Murasakino neighborhood, a townhouse the owner restored with its wide earthen-floor entry, exposed ceiling beams, and a courtyard garden tucked at the back. The owner's path to soba began with a single bowl of handmade soba he ate at a shop in Hida-Takayama that stayed with him. He approached that shop's master hoping to apprentice, but was turned away with the advice that there was no point in simply copying someone else — he should try it himself, and the master would help when needed. He had been working in advertising, so rather than a formal apprenticeship he taught himself, reading everything he could find on soba and eating at shops around the country while practicing at home for about two years, before opening Kanei in December 1999. · The shop's stated approach is to make everything carefully and to offer thoughtful, attentive hospitality, even if that means guests sometimes wait a while. places.chef: owner-chef, sommelier · 西陣 (Nishijin), Kyoto — Imadegawa area · Sobaya Nikora opened in 2003 in Kyoto's Nishijin district, founded by a husband-and-wife team who set out to run a place small enough that care could reach every individual guest. The husband, a former management consultant, spent eight years as head chef at his wife's family soba restaurant in Gifu before the couple struck out on their own. They settled into a renovated traditional townhouse (machiya) and gave it a quietly modern interior. The name nods to the painter Nicolas de Staël, a favorite of theirs, whose work is echoed in the space. · The couple wanted to revive the Edo-period custom of lingering over soba-mae and a drink before the noodles arrive — but reimagined for today. Rather than holding rigidly to tradition, they built a 'contemporary soba-mae' that borrows freely from Japanese, Italian, French, and Chinese cooking while keeping flavors simple and deep. The aim throughout is an unhurried space where grown-ups feel genuinely at ease, with the same care given to ingredients, room, and tableware. · Stone-ground, hand-milled, hand-cut 100% buckwheat soba (石臼粗引き手打ち十割蕎麦). The owner hails from Shinshu (Nagano Prefecture), one of Japan's great soba heartlands, where he grew up eating soba and developed a determination to treat this everyday food as something worth refining. Before opening Hanamomo he trained at a soba restaurant in Yamanashi. The shop is a modest two-floor space with only a handful of seats, and the work is genuinely hands-on: every morning from the early hours the owner stone-grinds buckwheat for the day, milling only as much of the autumn-harvested, hulled buckwheat as he needs and hand-cutting the noodles fresh. · Take soba, a humble everyday food, and elevate it through care without losing its accessibility: grind the flour fresh each morning, cut by hand, and let good buckwheat and the seasons do the talking. places.chef: owner, soba chef · Shichiku, Kita Ward, Kyoto · Tucked into a quiet Shichiku residential street north of Kitayama, Ogawa is a small handmade-soba shop opened in 2003 inside a renovated old Kyoto house. Its frontage is so understated that you would barely know it is a restaurant. It is run as an intimate, husband-and-wife-style operation with only about a dozen seats, open for lunch only and closing the moment the day's soba sells out. The owner is said to have learned in the lineage of the celebrated soba master Takahashi Kunihiro (of 'Okina'), and that pedigree shows in the work: the buckwheat is stone-milled in-house from domestic grain (sourced from Gunma), and only as much soba as can be eaten that day is cut that day. · Make only what can be milled and cut fresh each day, and serve it until it runs out. The little shop sits on Imadegawa-dori on the way up toward Ginkaku-ji and the Philosopher's Path; tourists fill it at lunch while locals come in the evening, and a queue often forms outside. · The owner believes the maker's frame of mind is part of the craft. places.chef: 秋岡誠 (Makoto Akioka) · owner, second-generation proprietor · Kyoto, Japan · Kissa Tyrol opened in 1968 near Nijōjō (Nijo Castle) in Kyoto's Nakagyō Ward, founded by a husband-and-wife team. The owner was an avid mountaineer, and he wanted the shop to feel like a mountain lodge — so the interior is full of warm wood, with a wooden chandelier and European touches such as the red-and-black striped awning and decorative ironwork over the windows. The founder's brother, a carpenter, traveled around Kyoto gathering ideas to build the distinctive woodwork and decorations, while the founder's wife designed the shop's logo and matchboxes, which are still beloved by visitors today. The café is now run by the second generation, Makoto Akioka, together with his family. It celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2018. The shop weathered a hard stretch in the late 1990s when subway construction redirected foot traffic away from the area, then found a devoted new audience after a 2011 NHK drama featured it as the lead character's regular haunt. It has deep ties to the Kyoto theater troupe Europa Kikaku and turns up often on TV and in magazines, but it has kept its quiet, nostalgic, neighborhood feel. …

places.chef: owner, mama · Kyoto, Japan (Higashikujo, Minami-ku) · Junkissa Minami opened in 1984 (Showa 59), the same year Kyoto Station's Hachijo-guchi Avanti complex first opened its doors, and it has been quietly serving travelers and neighborhood regulars from the building ever since. The mama who runs it opened the shop when she was just 23 years old, and decades on she still presides over the counter. Step in from the narrow entrance and the room opens up into a deep, elegant space hung with ornate crystal chandeliers, a true Showa-era pure-kissaten preserved inside a modern station building. Regulars describe the hosts as genuinely warm and attentive, the kind who make you want to linger over a cup of coffee. · A classic Showa kissaten known for its retro drinks and homey light meals: cream soda, cola, a fresh-squeezed lemon squash served in distinctive flower-footed retro glassware, and blend coffee, alongside plates of yakimeshi (fried rice with soup), omurice, mushroom spaghetti, royal toast, and a much-loved homemade curry rice, including an egg-topped version where the raw yolk is stirred through the roux and rice for a richer flavor.

For more than half a century it has quietly watched over daily life in Kyoto, drawing a mix of nearby market workers, neighborhood regulars, and travelers. The room leans into classic pure-coffeehouse character: vintage wooden tables, red velvet chairs, and large glass windows that frame the riverside cherry trees and the changing seasons. It is very much an adults' cafe by design, built around calm and unhurried time. places.chef: cafe, bookshop, vegetable shop · Kyoto · OyOy opened in June 2020 on the first floor of the Shinpuhkan complex by Karasuma Oike Station as a hybrid bookshop, cafe and vegetable shop. It is a collaboration between Saka no Tochu (坂ノ途中), a Kyoto organic-vegetable company that sources seasonal produce grown without pesticides or chemical fertilizers from partner farms, and Oraido (鴎来堂), the team behind Kamome Books in Kagurazaka, Tokyo, who curate the in-store library. · The name OyOy (oioi) evokes an unhurried pace - gradually and gently bringing vegetables and books into everyday life. The shop treats vegetables as living things, each with its own flavor, form and daily change, and pairs them with a curated shelf of books on food, farming and travel to enrich daily life. · The signature OyOy Seasonal Vegetable Plate, built entirely from plant-based seasonal vegetables and changing with what the farms harvest, alongside homemade desserts like seasonal tofu douhua and carrot cake, in-house fruit cordials, and Umi no Mukou coffee from Saka no Tochu's coffee division.

places.chef: community space / café, bookstore, event and workshop venue · Kyoto, Japan · Social Kitchen opened in September 2010 in a building just outside the south gate of Shokoku-ji temple in Kamigyo-ku, Kyoto. It was created by the Kyoto collective Hanare, which had been running a weekly community café since 2006. Conceived as a '21st-century community center,' the three-floor space pairs a ground-floor café and bookstore (Not Pillar Books) with a second-floor event hall for lectures, discussions, workshops and exhibitions, and a third-floor shared office for designers, programmers and art groups. · The café is framed as 'a project exploring the possibilities that expand from food.' It emphasizes locally grown ingredients and a deliberately low-waste system, treating eating as part of a broader practice of community, sustainability and dialogue rather than just a meal. · Daily-changing lunch plates, soups, curries (including plant-based dishes such as a South Indian bean curry), plus cakes, cookies and drinks served in a relaxed café-and-bookstore setting.

Treat as "ask" — no dedicated GF handling confirmed.

places.chef: University co-op cafeteria, Public-accessible campus dining hall · On Kyoto University's Yoshida campus · Cafeteria Rene is a Kyoto University Co-op dining hall on the 2nd floor of the west-side co-op building known as 'Rene.' places.chef: bakery, bagel specialist · Kyoto, Japan · Browny Bread & Bagels is a well-loved Kyoto bagel specialist that began on Kitaoji-dori in the north of the city before relocating in 2016 to its current spot in the Shogoin neighborhood of Sakyo-ku, a short walk south of the Higashioji and Marutamachi intersection near Heian Shrine and Kyoto Zoo. · The bakers emphasize carefully selected ingredients and extended, long-time fermentation to bring out the dough's fragrance, flavor and texture rather than relying on heavy fillings, with everything baked fresh on site each day. · Bagels above all: the shop keeps 20-30 varieties in stock at any time, made from domestic wheat with long fermentation and house-made yeast for a chewy, moist crumb and a deep wheat aroma. Signature flavors run from a popular cinnamon-apple-walnut with cream cheese to gorgonzola with honey and walnuts, kinako-mochi with red bean, sweet-potato cream cheese and bacon-cheese, alongside other savory breads. Bagels are graded by texture (firmer T-60 vs. softer T-70).

places.chef: Dai Okonogi (小此木 大) · owner, chef · From Aichi Prefecture, Japan; based in Kyoto · TADKA's owner-chef, Dai Okonogi (小此木 大), originally from Aichi Prefecture, trained at Mughal, a long-established Indian restaurant in Kyoto, before opening TADKA1 in 2012 as a street-stall-style South Indian lunch spot on Oshikoji-dori. places.chef: owner · 一乗寺, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · Opened in 2011 on Ichijoji's famous "Ramen Street" (ラーメン街道) in Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, Menya Gokkei staked out its own corner of one of Japan's most competitive ramen districts. The name 極鶏 ("Gokkei") fuses 極 (extreme/perfected) with 鶏 (chicken), and the shop has stayed laser-focused on a single idea ever since. · A one-bowl, one-idea shop: rather than chase variety, Gokkei pours everything into perfecting a single, unmistakable chicken broth — its own self-described 'one-of-a-kind soup to savor.' · The signature 極鶏 鶏だく: an ultra-concentrated chicken paitan so thick it is often described as 'doro-kei' (muddy) and famously dense enough that a spoon can stand upright in it. Chicken carcasses are simmered to an extreme, near-pottage consistency to create what the shop calls a 'soup you eat rather than drink.' Variations build on the same base: 赤だく (fiery red chili), 黒だく (fragrant black mayu garlic oil), and 魚だく (a fish-infused twist).

places.chef: 西岡津世志 (Nishioka Tsuyoshi) · founder, chef · Kyoto · Founded in October 2006 in the student town of Ichijoji, this is widely regarded as the pioneer of Kansai-style Jiro ramen. places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (Emmachi / Nishinokyo, Nakagyo-ku) · A small, quietly run ramen counter a few minutes from JR Emmachi station, kept deliberately modest: just nine seats along an L-shaped counter, worked by the owner and one assistant. Despite earning a Michelin Bib Gourmand (2016), the shop has held onto unusually low prices, with the basic soy bowl staying around 650 yen while most acclaimed ramen shops have drifted well past 1,000 yen. · Refinement without spectacle: a restrained, balanced bowl at an everyday price, prioritizing clean broth and good noodles over flash or markup. · An 'assari' (light, clean) style: the soy-sauce ramen layers a chicken-bone base with Japanese dashi, while the salt (shio) ramen pairs chicken and seafood stock with a lift of yuzu. places.chef: ramen shop · Kyoto · 麺屋 猪一 opened on 3 July 2013 and relocated on 1 May 2019 to its current spot on Teramachi-dori in Shimogyo-ku, just south of Shijo near Kawaramachi. places.chef: owner · Opened in 2010 in a quiet residential stretch of Ichijoji, Kyoto's famed 'ramen street,' a two-minute walk from Eizan Railway's Ichijoji Station, and grew almost entirely by word of mouth into one of the area's most queued-for tsukemen counters. A small counter of about a dozen seats (twelve) wraps around the open kitchen, so you eat just steps from where the bowls are built. · A deliberately narrow menu — essentially three tsukemen (standard fish-and-pork-bone, spicy, and curry) plus toppings and rice — reflecting a focus on doing one thing exceptionally rather than chasing variety. · The signature is the 魚介豚骨つけ麺 — silky, chewy extra-thick house-made noodles (milled from Izawa whole-grain flour) served beside a deeply concentrated pork-bone-and-fish dipping broth, balanced with fish powder, oil and a touch of spice. places.gfd: A tsukemen specialist built around house-made extra-thick wheat noodles dipped in a rich pork-bone-and-fish broth that is virtually always thickened/seasoned with wheat-containing elements. There is no gluten-free noodle, no separate prep, and no indication of allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs or those needing strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: The entire menu is centered on pork-bone (tonkotsu) and fish (gyokai) broth, with meat and egg toppings. There are no vegan or vegetarian bowls. Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.

places.chef: owner, head chef · Tokyo (Jiro lineage, founded 1968) · Ramen Jiro Kyoto opened on April 2, 2017, as a fully sanctioned 直系 (direct-lineage) branch of the legendary Tokyo Ramen Jiro empire — for several years it stood as the only direct Jiro branch in all of western Japan (until a Kyushu branch later opened). The proprietor trained at the Jimbocho (神保町) Jiro in Tokyo before bringing the style to Ichijoji, a neighborhood already famous as one of Kyoto's great ramen streets. · Pure, unapologetic Jiro: enormous portions, bold pork-fat richness, and an efficient eat-and-go counter rhythm. The shop keeps the old-school 二郎 atmosphere intact rather than softening it for a tourist crowd. · The classic Jiro bowl: a mountain of thick, flat, chewy hand-cut wheat noodles under a tangle of boiled bean sprouts and cabbage, slabs of thick-cut chashu pork, and a rich pork-and-back-fat soy broth. Diners customize at the counter with the Jiro 'call' — ninniku (garlic), yasai (extra veg), abura (back fat), karame (extra tare) — and finish with counter condiments like coarse pepper and chili.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. Jiro-style ramen is built on thick wheat noodles, a wheat-based soy-sauce tare, and a pork-and-back-fat broth — all standard wheat-containing components. There is no gluten-free menu, no separate preparation, and the kitchen is a single shared boil-and-assemble line. Celiac and gluten-sensitive diners should not eat here.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The broth is a heavy pork (and back-fat) stock, bowls are built around large chunks of chashu pork, and the tare is animal/soy-sauce based. There are no vegetable or plant-based bowls; even toppings like extra vegetables sit in pork broth. Vegans cannot eat here.

places.chef: owner · ムジコ (Mujiko) is one of the very few abura soba specialists in Kyoto — a city far better known for its kotteri ramen than for brothless oil noodles — which makes it something of a local curiosity. It sits on Senbon-dori in the Kamigyo ward, a short walk from Nijo Station, as a small counter-style shop (it shares its building with a spice-curry spot). · A focused, do-one-thing-well abura soba bar: a tight menu of four variations on the same idea, customizable at the table, with portion size left up to the diner at no extra charge. · The signature is the standard 油そば (abura soba): chewy medium-thick wheat noodles tossed at the bottom of the bowl with a special soy-sauce-based tare and flavored oil, no soup. places.vgd: Not a vegan-friendly shop. No vegan or vegetarian bowl is advertised. A vegan diner could not be accommodated with the standard menu.
places.hours: Tue–Sun, holidays, and days before holidays 11:30–15:30 (food last order 15:00) / 18:00–22:30 (food last order 22:00); closed Mon. (Note: Tabelog also lists closed Thu with dinner last order 21:30, so confirming before visiting is recommended.)

places.chef: 田口有司（Taguchi Yuji） · Long-established Kyoto ramen institution, Pre-dawn opening near Kyoto Station · Kyoto Station / Takabashi, Shimogyo-ku · Born in 1947 near Kyoto Station at the spot locals call "Takabashi," this is the original shop of the celebrated Daiichi Asahi lineage of Kyoto ramen. It started life as a humble eatery (Asahi Shokudo / 旭食堂) and was renamed 第一旭 in 1956 as it became a dedicated ramen specialist, opening before dawn to feed early-morning workers and travelers near the station — a habit that survives today in its famous 6 a.m. opening. · A long-protected, continually refined old-school taste ("守り続け、磨き続けてきた老舗の味") built on careful sourcing — Kyoto-grown Kujo negi and mung-bean sprouts, raw soy sauce from a long-established Kyoto (Fushimi) maker, and char siu from a single specific grade of domestic pork chosen for its lean, clean balance of fat and meat so the soup stays gentle on the palate. · The signature 特製ラーメン (chuka soba): a clear yet deeply savory pork-bone broth seasoned with raw Kyoto soy sauce, piled with thinly sliced char siu, a generous tangle of Kujo green onions, and bean sprouts, over medium-thick dried-aged wheat noodles.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The signature 中華そば is wheat ramen noodles (medium-thick blended-flour noodles aged dry, by Kondo Seimen) in a pork-bone broth seasoned with a wheat-based Kyoto soy sauce tare (生醤油 from Fushimi / Goko Shoyu). Noodles, tare, and gyoza all contain wheat; there is no gluten-free option and no indication of allergen accommodation. Avoid if you require strict gluten-free.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The entire menu is built around a pork-bone (豚骨) broth, char siu (roast pork), and pork-fat finish, with soy-sauce tare; toppings include kujo negi, bean sprouts, menma and pork. No vegetable/plant-based broth or vegan bowl is offered.

In April 2022 he relocated the
places.chef: Sodeoka (袖岡) · owner, chef · Kyoto · The shop's name とうひち is written 藤七 and read 'touhichi' in the Kyoto dialect. After leaving a corporate career in his late 30s, the owner (Sodeoka) trained for about four years at the renowned Kyoto ramen house 京都千丸しゃかりき (Kyoto Senmaru Shakariki) before opening his own counter in a quiet residential pocket of Kita Ward in March 2015. In April 2022 he relocated the shop to its current spot a short walk from Shugakuin Station, into premises that had previously housed his sister shop Suguru. · A restrained, transparency-first aesthetic: a simple-looking but deeply layered broth meant to slide cleanly across the palate, with the raw-pressed-soy-sauce chicken-clear style being the direction the owner settled on during his training years. · The signature bowl is the tori-shoyu raa-men: a crystal-clear chicken broth (tori-seitan) seasoned with raw-pressed nama-age soy sauce and gilded with fragrant chicken oil, topped with two kinds of chashu, thick menma and chopped green onion. The repertoire also runs to a richer tori-paitan, a niboshi (sardine) seafood bowl, and tsuke-soba dipping noodles served with a kombu-steeped water bath for the noodles.
places.gfd: This is a classic ramen shop: wheat noodles served in chicken broth with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare. The signature bowls are built on a raw-pressed soy sauce (nama-age shoyu) chicken-clear broth, and Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat. With wheat noodles plus a wheat-based tare, there is no gluten-free option here and the kitchen is not set up for celiac-safe service. No gluten-free claims were found on any page; treat as not suitable for celiac/gluten-free diners.
places.vgd: Every signature bowl is built on a chicken broth (tori-seitan clear soup or tori-paitan), finished with chicken oil, and topped with pork chashu. There is no vegan or vegetable-broth ramen on the menu, and no vegan options were found on any page.
places.hours: Mon, Wed-Sun 11:00-14:30, 18:00-21:00; Tuesday closed. Ticket-vending-machine order; lunch and dinner service may end early when sold out.

places.chef: Ido (井戸) · proprietor · 京都 / Kyoto (Tsubame-Sanjo style of Niigata, reinterpreted for Kyoto palates) · Seabura no Kami began almost by accident. After about three months working as a black-suited host in Gion, the founder found his afternoons free and decided to run a ramen shop again — but only at lunch to start. He chose Niigata's Tsubame-Sanjo style as the signature precisely because nothing like it existed in Kyoto at the time, and the city had no real niboshi (dried-sardine) ramen culture either. A tasting trip to Hakkaisan in Takatsuki sparked the idea ('this is interesting'), and after consulting the noodle maker Teigaku (棣鄂) and the owner of Ken Ramen's Yamauchi shop, he committed to the concept. · Indulgent but not heavy: refuse to merely imitate Niigata's Tsubame ramen and instead build a distinct identity by obsessively refining the back fat itself, aiming for an approachable bowl where the niboshi is present but restrained. · 背脂煮干そば (seabura niboshi soba) — back-fat dried-sardine ramen. places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The owner is a Shinpuku Saikan man through and through: he started training at that
places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto, in the Shinpuku Saikan lineage · Menya Ryugen opened in July 2016 on Ichijoji's quieter back lane, just off the neighborhood's famous ramen street, in the space once occupied by another ramen shop (Menya Kagari) that had closed the year before. The other half of the order is the yakimeshi (fried rice), seasoned dark and aromatic with soy; …

places.chef: owner-operator · A small independent noodle shop tucked into the basement of the Zuisho Building near Doshisha University's Shinmachi campus, just a short walk from Imadegawa Station. It bills itself as the only specialty shop in Kyoto City devoted to shiru-nashi tantanmen (brothless dan dan noodles), and draws a steady student crowd at lunch. · The shop emphasizes handmade chili oil and its own custom spice blend, and a commitment to locally sourced (地産地消) Kyoto ingredients, aiming for a balance where the umami of the ingredients is still felt amid the spice. · The signature bowl is the shiru-nashi tantanmen: wheat noodles tossed in a house-blended sauce of carefully made chili oil and several spices, finished with the aromatic fragrance of sesame so that umami comes through within the heat. The kitchen also makes a mapo-style noodle (汁なし麻婆麺) and a standalone mapo tofu, both with adjustable spice levels, plus rice that pairs with the spicy sauces.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The core dishes are wheat noodles dressed in a sesame-and-chili-oil tantan sauce, and the menu centers on tantanmen and mabo-men (mapo-style noodles) — all wheat-based. Not suitable for celiacs.

Ichijoji is one of Japan's most famous ramen battlegrounds, lined with shops along what locals call the
places.chef: owner-operator · Hokuriku (Ishikawa/Fukui) origins; established in Kyoto Ichijoji in 2011. · Ikedaya began life outside Kyoto, in the Hokuriku region (its first shop was in Nonoichi, Ishikawa), before the owner brought the shop to Kyoto's Ichijoji district in 2011. The shop later expanded with branches in Fukui and in the Osaka/Amagasaki area, but the small Ichijoji counter near Eizan Railway's Ichijoji Station remains its spiritual home. · Ikedaya is proudly an 'inspired' shop rather than an official Jiro branch: the owner never trained at the original and instead developed his own interpretation of the style, chasing maximum pork richness and volume on his own terms. places.gfd: Not safe for gluten-free or celiac diners. places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Takamatsu built its name on tsukemen (dipping noodles) at a time when the style was still uncommon in Kyoto, and the main shop remains a small counter-driven room where the noodles take center stage.
places.chef: tsukemen specialist, noodle maker · Founded in 2011 in the Shijo-Karasuma district of central Kyoto, this is the flagship (honten) of the Takamatsu noodle house, which has since grown to five shops around the city. · Takamatsu built its name on tsukemen (dipping noodles) at a time when the style was still uncommon in Kyoto, and the main shop (on Takoyakushi-dori near Shijo-Karasuma) remains a small counter-driven room where the noodles take center stage. · The house motto is 'a single bowl of happiness, every day' (毎日に、一杯の幸せを) — an everyday, repeatable comfort rather than a special-occasion meal. · The signature bowl is a tsukemen of thin, roughly 2mm stone-ground whole-grain noodles served with a clean, unthickened chicken-and-seafood dipping broth that blends select chicken with katsuo, saba and scallop. The kitchen leans on whole-grain flour milled from Nagano-grown wheat, giving the noodles a rustic, wheat-forward character closer to country soba than typical glossy tsukemen noodles.
places.gfd: The entire concept is built on stone-ground whole-grain wheat noodles, and the chicken-seafood tsukemen broth is finished with a tare that almost certainly contains wheat-based shoyu. There is no gluten-free menu and no indication of a dedicated preparation area. This is not a safe choice for anyone with celiac disease or a wheat allergy. Confirm directly before any visit if cross-contact is a concern.
places.vgd: The signature broth is an animal-based chicken-and-fish (鶏魚介) stock combining poultry with katsuo, saba and scallop, so the core offering is not vegan and not vegetarian. No plant-based ramen option is advertised. A strict vegan or vegetarian cannot eat the standard bowls here.

places.chef: owner-operator · Kyoto (Karasuma Oike, Nakagyo-ku) · 麺屋 優光 is a small, independent ramen shop tucked into the Karasuma Oike office district of central Kyoto. Its owner trained at the celebrated Osaka ramen shop 人類みな麺類 (Jinrui Mina Menrui) before opening here. The space deliberately feels more like a bright, stylish cafe than a typical ramen counter, with seats at the counter downstairs and tables upstairs, and it welcomes solo diners and a notably high share of women. · The shop frames itself around caring for the customer during the short time they spend eating — making a quick bowl of ramen feel like a considered, hospitable experience. · A shellfish-based 中華そば (kai-dashi ramen) that is genuinely rare for Kyoto: the soup layers the umami of shellfish (clams and other shellfish) into a soy-based tare for a clean but pronounced, slightly sweet-savory profile. The three regular bowls are named after types of bamboo — 淡竹 (Hachiku), 真竹 (Madake) and 黒竹 (Kurochiku) — with Hachiku the most popular, finished with several thick slices of soft, low-temperature seared rare pork charshiu.
places.gfd: The house noodles are made fresh daily from a blend of whole-wheat and udon flour, and the broth uses a soy-sauce (shoyu) based tare, which almost always contains wheat. This is a wheat-noodle, wheat-tare ramen and is not safe for celiac diners; no gluten-free option is indicated.
places.vgd: All bowls are built on a shellfish (oyster, clam, shrimp) dashi combined with a soy-based tare, and the signature topping is low-temperature seared rare pork charshiu. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu.

places.chef: 上嶋 泰範 (Yasunori Ueshima) · owner, chef · 下京区西七条、JR丹波口駅から徒歩約10分。2014年5月開業。 · The owner trained at 俺のラーメンあっぱれ屋 (Ore no Ramen Appareya), the famous ramen shop tucked in the hills of Kyoto, before striking out on his own and opening this shop in the city. He kept the mentor shop's menu DNA — even the dish names nod to Appareya (こくまろ塩 to its こくとん, 濁とろ塩 to its 濁とん, うるとらつけ麺 to its スーパーつけ麺) — while building a distinct identity of his own. · A counter-focused, single-diner-friendly shop (おひとり様専門店) that opens unusually early at 10:30 and runs a flavored-oil 'no-leftover' approach so guests can vary the soup's character as they eat — the kind of detail-obsessed, owner-run craft inherited from its Appareya training. · The signature is the うるとらつけ麺 (Ultra Tsukemen): a濃厚豚骨, foam-rich dipping broth carrying assertive salt and spice, paired with house-made chewy flat noodles with a smooth finish. places.chef: owner-operated counter tsukemen shop · Kyoto (Nakagyo-ku, Rokkaku-dori / Shinkyogoku) · A small, tucked-away tsukemen specialist on Rokkaku-dori in the Shinkyogoku/Teramachi shopping warren, just a short walk from Shijo-Kawaramachi and Kyoto City Hall-mae Station. The room is famously compact — an L-shaped counter of roughly ten seats and a single four-top table, so tight that a separate rear door is used to manage the flow of customers — which gives it the feel of a true neighborhood noodle den. · Straightforwardly delicious, honest tsukemen — chewy house-made noodles in generous portions with broth that clings to every strand, the kind of bowl regulars return to rather than a one-time novelty. · The signature bowl is the gyokai shoyu tsukemen (魚介醤油つけ麺): self-made, thick wavy noodles cut with whole-grain wheat, given free in a large portion, dipped into a concentrated seafood-and-pork shoyu broth balanced between animal umami and dried sardine/bonito notes, finished with tender chashu and a dusting of aonori. The shop also runs ramen, cold mixed noodles, a miso-tantan tsukemen, and rotating limited bowls.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free and not celiac-safe. The house specialty is self-made thick wavy noodles made with whole wheat flour (自家製の全粒粉入り加水麺), served with a seafood-and-pork shoyu dipping broth that uses wheat-based soy sauce tare. Both the noodles and the tare contain wheat; broths are animal/fish based. No gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or published allergy program were found. A celiac or strict gluten-avoider cannot eat the core dishes here.
places.vgd: No vegan options. The kitchen is built around fish (dried sardine/bonito) and pork/chicken broths, with chashu pork as a standard topping; the signature is a seafood-pork shoyu tsukemen. No plant-based broth or vegan bowl is offered. A vegan diner has nothing suitable on the menu.

places.chef: owner · Ichijoji, Kyoto (parent shop Yume wo Katare) · Opened in 2009 as a spinoff of the famous Ichijoji Jiro-inspired shop "夢を語れ" (Yume wo Katare), this Fushimi flagship grew into one of the standard-bearers of the Kansai Jiro-kei (Jiro-style) ramen scene and went on to spawn multiple branches across the region. · Big, generous, made-to-order satisfaction: the kitchen prizes the sharp cut of the soy tare layered over deep umami, and lets each customer dial in the bowl with the classic Jiro call of garlic, vegetables and fat for an "overwhelmingly satisfying" finish. · A thunderous Jiro-style bowl built on house-made flat, extra-thick noodles (offered 200g/300g/400g) and a non-emulsified pork-bone-and-soy broth, piled with mountains of vegetables, garlic and back-fat. places.gfd: This is a Jiro-style ramen shop: thick house-made wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth seasoned with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is virtually always wheat-based. places.chef: ramen shop · Kyoto, near Kyoto Station (Shimogyo-ku). · A specialist ramen counter a short walk from Kyoto Station, Kitada built its reputation on one idea done very well: a clear, fragrant broth drawn entirely from shellfish. The shop opens early — its doors are up at 7:00 a.m. — which has made it a favorite stop for 'asa-ra' (morning ramen), with a line of regulars and travelers already forming mid-morning. · Let the shellfish speak — a clear, delicate broth that is light enough to drink in the morning yet still eats like a full bowl of ramen. · Kai-dashi shio ramen — a clear, salt-seasoned broth simmered from generous amounts of hamaguri (hard clam), asari (littleneck clam) and hotate (scallop), giving a clean, sweet shellfish umami rather than the usual pork-bone heaviness. The signature 'specialty' bowl and the 蛤らぁ麺 (hamaguri ramen) lead the menu; the regular 貝だし麺 layers in a house-made aromatic shellfish oil for a richer hit. Straight thin noodles milled from Hokkaido 'yumechikara' wheat, pork-loin chashu, red onion and green sprouts round out the bowl, with miso (貝だし辛味噌) and a classic chuka-soba also offered.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles — the shop uses Hokkaido "yumechikara" wheat for its straight thin noodles — and a salt (shio) tare that, like nearly all Japanese ramen seasoning, is very likely to contain wheat-based ingredients. The shellfish dashi broth itself (hamaguri, asari, hotate) is naturally gluten-light, but the noodles and tare make the dish unsafe for anyone with celiac disease or wheat allergy. No gluten-free menu, no separate prep, and no dedicated equ…
places.vgd: This is a shellfish-broth ramen specialist — every signature bowl is built on a clam/scallop (hamaguri, asari, hotate) clear dashi, and bowls are topped with pork-loin chashu. There is no vegan or vegetarian broth, and no plant-based bowl was found on the menu. Not a destination for vegan or vegetarian diners.

places.chef: ramen shop, local neighborhood eatery · Kyoto · Ebisuya opened in the Shimogamo neighborhood in January 2013, calling itself a maker of "original Kyoto ramen" (元祖京都らーめん) — a deliberate nod to the back-fat chicken-and-soy-sauce style that defined the city's noodle culture before the wave of creamy tonkotsu shops. · The shop is unapologetically nostalgic — it preserves the older Kyoto ramen identity its owner grew up with rather than chasing modern trends. · The signature bowl is a chicken-gara soy-sauce ramen crowned with pork back-fat (背脂チャッチャ系), built on thin, slightly curly Kyoto-style noodles; a tonkotsu version rounds out the menu. places.chef: 山内 健吾 (Kengo Yamauchi) · owner-chef · Kyoto, Shimogyo Ward (Suzaku / Umekoji area) · 拳ラーメン (Kobushi Ramen) sits a few minutes' walk from Umekoji Park near Umekoji-Kyotonishi Station in Kyoto's Shimogyo Ward. Run by owner-chef Kengo Yamauchi, a former washoku (Japanese-cuisine) cook, the shop was renamed and relocated from its earlier incarnation 'こぶ志,' opening at its current spot on March 28, 2011, and has grown into one of the area's most respected ramen counters. places.chef: ramen shop · Kyoto (Seabura no Kami group; flagship in Mibu, Shimogyo-ku) · This is the Fushimi outpost of Seabura no Kami, the Kyoto ramen group whose flagship is in Mibu (Shimogyo), with additional shops including a Nishiki location. Set right by Fushimi Station in southern Kyoto, the Goriki branch grew its own identity rather than simply copying the main shop, and at one point reworked its concept toward a rougher, more forceful 'Goriki' (powerful) style with notes borrowed from the bold ramen culture of Tsubame-Sanjo. · An approachable, Kyoto-tuned read on Jiro: serious volume and back fat, but tempered — finer-than-typical Jiro noodles and a lighter, less heavy broth (often with grated fresh ginger offered in place of mandatory raw garlic) so newcomers can enjoy a Jiro-style bowl, while the renovated 'Goriki' direction keeps it satisfying for hardcore fans. · Kami Jiro — the shop's own take on Jiro-style ramen, served with a dedicated extra-thick, heavily-crinkled noodle in 200g/300g/400g sizes, over a pork-and-fish broth crowned with back fat that's been seasoned with Kyoto Gokko soy sauce for a sweet, umami finish. places.chef: ramen shop, tsukemen shop · 京都発の地元店 · A Kyoto-grown ramen shop. The first 一粒万倍 opened near Sanjo Kawaramachi in 2019, and this Teramachi branch followed in January 2022, on Teramachi street just south of Shijo near Kyoto-Kawaramachi station; sister shops have since opened in Saiin and Gion. The name 一粒万倍 comes from 一粒万倍日, an auspicious day in the Japanese calendar meaning that a single grain of rice multiplies ten-thousandfold — a wish for prosperity that the shop extends to its guests. · Bringing good fortune to the diner — the shop leans into its auspicious name to make a bowl of ramen feel lucky as well as satisfying. · A light, refined (淡麗系) clear broth built on duck and branded Daisen chicken (大山どり, from Tottori), served as both 醤油 (soy) and 塩 (salt) bowls. places.chef: owner-operator · Kyoto · Opened in 2015 in the Shijo-Karasuma area of central Kyoto, Menya Mitsuru built its reputation on a single idea done well: a rich, collagen-heavy chicken paitan broth. places.chef: tantanmen specialist, counter shop · Kyoto (Gosho-minami / Sakaicho-Ibikawa), opened spring 2024. · 京都担担麺 金鵄楼 (Kinshiro) opened on March 25, 2024 in the quiet Gosho-minami neighborhood at the Sakaicho-Ibikawa corner of Nakagyo Ward, a stylish counter-only shop (about six seats) that quickly drew lunchtime lines soon after opening. · A focused single-dish specialist: do tantanmen well, let guests dial in their own heat and numbing spice, and keep an intimate counter where solo diners feel welcome. · Tantanmen offered three ways - with broth (汁あり), without broth (汁なし), and chilled (冷やし). places.chef: Sasaki Koji · owner-chef, family-run kitchen · Kyoto (Gion lineage, Beijing-style Chinese cuisine) · Seikatei opened in 1982 in the quiet temple district near Ginkaku-ji. Its roots run back to 盛京亭 (Seikyotei), a Beijing-style restaurant founded in 1951 in the heart of Gion's hanamachi (geisha district). The founder's father served as head chef at Seikyotei, and the son went on to open this independent shop, carrying most of the original menu with it. · A Kyoto take on Chinese food: because the original Gion shop cooked for geiko and refined patrons, it deliberately dialed back heavy aromatics like garlic and excess oil. Seikatei keeps that restraint — light white-pressed soybean oil (shirashime-yu), local Matsui-brewery sake instead of cooking wine, and clean, delicate flavors over punch. · Goma-gyoza (sesame dumplings): roasted sesame is kneaded right into the wrapper, with a filling of only cabbage, Chinese chives, pork and sake, then pan-fried in a heavy cast iron pan until the surface turns crisp. It began as an off-menu request from a regular and became the house signature.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation indicated. The signature sesame gyoza even has roasted sesame kneaded into a wheat wrapper. Not suitable for celiac diners; no dedicated handling found.

places.chef: Tsuchida Naoki (owner) · owner-operator, noodle shop · Murasaki / Shin-Omiya shopping street, Kita-ku, Kyoto, near Daitoku-ji · Founded in 1939 (Showa 14) as a coffee shop, the business reinvented itself during wartime as a Western-style restaurant and, after the war, became a specialist Chinese noodle shop. Traces of those earlier lives still linger on the menu in the form of kissaten-style cafe items kept on as a nod to the past. · Quietly perfectionist about the basics: the cold-noodle sauce is built on honjozo vinegar of the grade used in Kyoto's high-end kaiseki kitchens, and the noodles themselves were dialed in over dozens of trial batches in collaboration with a local noodle maker so they would marry perfectly with the sauce. · The legendary cold noodles (冷麺) — roast pork, cucumber and seaweed over custom wheat noodles in a vinegar-and-sesame sauce. Unusually, the shop serves them year-round rather than only in summer, and roughly 90% of customers order them. The other pillar is a classic soy-based chuka-soba.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto — Gion / Higashiyama · にぼ魂 opened on August 8, 2025 in the heart of Gion, just north of Gion-Shijo Station off Nawate-dori, taking over a space that had until then housed a kasu-udon shop (かすうどん). It was conceived from the start as a deep-night niboshi-ramen stop — a bowl to land in after an evening out in Gion's bars and teahouses, when most kitchens have long closed, running from around 8pm into the early-morning hours. · Lean into the niboshi rather than tame it — a punchy, sea-forward bowl built for the late-night palate, served bright and clean in a small room. Diners can dial the flavor themselves with the tabletop kit of spiced tare, black and white pepper, and niboshi vinegar, and free extra-large noodle portions reward a hungry post-drinking crowd. · The signature is the Special Nibodamashii Ramen (特製にぼ魂ラーメン): an unapologetically bitter, dried-sardine (niboshi) broth ladled over thick, curly noodles, finished with marbled chashu, a soft-boiled egg, nori, and a single whole niboshi as garnish. The kitchen deliberately leaves the sardine heads and innards in the stock rather than removing them to soften the bitterness.
places.gfd: This is a niboshi (dried sardine) ramen specialist serving thick curly wheat noodles in a fish-based broth. places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (lineage from Daiei Ramen, Minami ward) · The original Ramen Daiei was founded in 1980 in Kyoto's Minami ward. The current owner is the founder's nephew — raised by his uncle from childhood and apprenticed to him for close to two decades — who then went independent and opened this Kawaramachi-Marutamachi shop around 1998 (it reached its 20th year in 2018) to carry the lineage forward. When the founder passed away in 2017, he left a charge to keep the recipe alive. · The founder's words guide the shop: 'ラーメンはスープが命' (the broth is the soul of ramen). The kitchen keeps the broth pure and clean - made only from premium pork and bones, with no cloudiness, bitterness, or gaminess - aiming for a refreshing, never-tiring bowl. · A clear, aromatic Kyoto-style shoyu tonkotsu ramen crowned with a mountain of freshly hand-sliced chashu and a generous heap of Kujo negi. The popular order is the shoyu chashu-men with extra negi; a miso version is also offered, and a yaki-meshi (fried rice) set rounds out the menu.

places.vgd: Every bowl is built on a pork-and-bone broth (described as crystal-clear shoyu tonkotsu made from premium Iga pork), and chashu pork is the signature topping. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu; even a plain bowl uses animal broth. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto (Kitashirakawa kei) · 東龍 opened in December 2000 in the Kitashirakawa neighborhood of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward. The owner had previously worked as a manager at Karako, a well-known ramen shop in Higashiyama, and brought that pedigree to his own counter on the quiet north-eastern edge of the city. · An emphasis on hand-made work and fresh ingredients runs through the kitchen, down to the rice — the owner serves Koshihikari grown on his family's farm in Kutsuki. · The signature bowl is 東龍そば, described as a kind of 'kaiseki in a bowl' — a creamy salt-based broth simmered from pork bone, chicken carcass, chicken-feet gelatin and around ten kinds of vegetables, served with house-made curly egg noodles, Kyotamba-highland pork-belly chashu and Kujo green onion. A second house specialty, 福仙楼そば, is a Taiwanese-street-stall-inspired pork-and-chicken paitan in a shoyu key with slow-braised tendon and minced pork over flatter, thicker egg noodles.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. Both signature bowls use house-made egg (wheat) noodles, and the 福仙楼そば is shoyu-seasoned (wheat-based soy sauce). Broths are pork-bone and chicken-gara based. places.chef: owner-operator · Yamashina, Kyoto · Yumenchu is a much-loved Yamashina tsukemen shop with a comeback story. The original shop near Miryoji closed for roughly three years while the owner recovered from an injury; it reopened on October 1, 2018, in a roomier space near Kyoto Pharmaceutical University, drawing a line of around 50 people on opening day. · Rather than chasing the heaviest possible broth, the shop aims for a cleaner, balanced dip where both the fish and pork-bone umami read clearly, with a touch of acidity and citrus, an approachable style meant to win over tsukemen newcomers as much as devotees. · Tsukemen only. The house bowl pairs thick, angular, homemade noodles with a fish-and-pork-bone broth, including a charred burnt-oil version (焦がしつけ麺) that adds aromatic depth. places.chef: noodle-factory-direct ramen shop, Kyoto-style ramen specialist · Minami-ku, Kyoto — near Jujo Station along Shin-Jujo-dori · A beloved old-guard Kyoto ramen shop founded in the early 1970s (1973, with some sources citing 1972), Ramen Fuji has fed the south-Kyoto neighborhood for over half a century. It is the flagship of a small local family of shops, with branches around the city (Fushimi Ote, Gojo, Fukuchiyama, Kyotanabe). · The shop's edge is the noodle itself: it is run as a direct outlet of Kondo Seimen (近藤製麺), the family noodle factory a few minutes' walk away. That factory has long supplied the noodles behind some of Kyoto's most storied ramen names, so the springy, well-cut house noodle is the heart of every bowl here. · A classic Kyoto-style pork-bone-and-soy bowl: a 豚骨醤油 broth in the clear (清湯) idiom — rich yet transparent, savory with a clean soy finish — piled with green onion and bean sprouts over thin, straight noodles. Beyond the standard ramen there is a 特製 (special), a miso version, and a menma bowl, with gyoza and a pork rice bowl (豚めし) on the side.

places.chef: owner-operator · Yamashina, Kyoto · Lee started life in May 2021 as 'Curry Shop Lee,' a curry-focused spot on the gaikanjō ring road in the Natsutsuji neighborhood of Yamashina, near Aeon Town. Over time the kitchen leaned more and more into noodles, and in May 2024 it fully rebranded into a ramen-and-mazesoba shop while keeping its curry roots front and center. · Curry expertise carried into the noodle bowl — the keema curry is built to be spice-forward but balanced, 'spicy without being overwhelming,' reflecting the shop's years as a curry kitchen. The clean, café-like counter room is a deliberate departure from the typical ramen-shop feel. · The signature bowl is the keema curry mazesoba: springy Y-shaped 'wing' noodles from the long-established Kyoto maker Teigaku (棣鄂) tossed with a layered keema curry, finished with egg yolk, cheese, house-made bacon, pork back fat, tomato and parsley. Staff ask each guest about garlic before serving it. Alongside it sit a gyokai-shoyu mazesoba and a Taiwan mazesoba, plus three ramen styles: tori-niboshi (chicken-sardine), tori-tonkotsu (rich chicken and pork bone), and gyokai tori-tonkotsu.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The core menu is wheat ramen and mazesoba noodles (sourced from Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku / 棣鄂) served with wheat-based shoyu and curry sauces. There is no indication staff can accommodate a gluten allergy.
places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian options. Ramen broths are chicken and pork-bone (and chicken-seafood) based; mazesoba and the keema curry use ground pork/meat, homemade bacon, egg yolk, cheese and pork back fat. There is no plant-based bowl on the menu.

places.chef: 平岡寛視 (Hiroshi Hiraoka) · producer, chef · An offshoot of the celebrated Sapporo shop Japanese Ramen Noodle Lab Q, brought to Kyoto as the brand's first Kansai venture; the Shijo-Karasuma shop (Nakagyo-ku) opened on April 9, 2022. · Producer Hiroshi Hiraoka built his reputation in Sapporo with Lab Q, known for crystal-clear, multi-layered broths. places.chef: noodle shop, maze-soba specialist · A branch of Menya Yamahide, whose main shop is in Nara. · An offshoot of a Nara maze-soba house, this Kyoto outpost opened on November 26, 2022 in the quiet Shogoin neighborhood near Kumano Shrine and Kyoto University Hospital, a short walk from Jingu-Marutamachi Station. places.chef: owner-proprietor (female proprietor, descendant of the geisha Takeka) · Gion, Kyoto · Takeka opened in 1966 at the foot of Gion Shinbashi, beside the Shirakawa stream, and has spent close to six decades cooking for the geiko and maiko, teahouse patrons, and locals of the district. places.chef: Hamamura Hozo (founder, 濱村保三); third-generation Hamamura Yoshiyuki (濱村吉行) · founder, third-generation owner-operator · Kyoto, Japan · Hamamura was founded in 1924 (Taisho 13) and is widely credited as the birthplace of Kyoto Chinese (kyo-chuka). What began as a humble noodle-and-Chinese shop grew into one of the city's defining culinary lineages, now run by the founder's grandson, the third-generation Hamamura Yoshiyuki. The Fuchomae branch sits across from the Kyoto Prefectural Office and moved to this Marutamachi spot from Kawaramachi around 2014. · Kyoto Chinese holds back the garlic and heavy oil of mainland Chinese cooking, leaning instead on chicken-bone and kombu dashi for a clean, restrained flavor. Their straightforward chuka-soba is the other anchor of the menu.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop is the realization of a 13-year dream for owner-chef Takuya Kozasa, who trained for 13 years at the influential Kyoto Jiro-style house 'ラーメン荘 地球規模で考えろ／そら' (Ramen Sho 'Chikyu-kibo de Kangaero' / Sora) before striking out on his own. It opened on October 6, 2025.
places.chef: 小笹琢也 (Takuya Kozasa) · owner, chef, noodle-maker · Kyoto (Nishi-Shichijo, Shimogyo Ward) — opened in the former premises of the ramen shop Akamon (赤もん) · The shop is the realization of a 13-year dream for owner-chef Takuya Kozasa, who trained for 13 years at the influential Kyoto Jiro-style house 'ラーメン荘 地球規模で考えろ／そら' (Ramen Sho 'Chikyu-kibo de Kangaero' / Sora) before striking out on his own. It opened on October 6, 2025, with 12 counter seats. · Despite the big, brawny Jiro format, the cooking aims for balance — the soy tare is kept deliberately restrained in saltiness to let the broth's natural pork sweetness come through, tuned toward Kyoto palates, with garlic and a touch of chili (一味) for punch. The chef keeps refining the recipe by tracking room temperature and humidity day to day. · Jiro-style (二郎系) ramen built on house-made extra-thick, hand-massaged noodles (極太手揉み麺) cut on the shop's own noodle machine, in a sweet-edged pork-bone broth crowned with mounded vegetables, back fat (アブラ), garlic, and thick chashu. places.gfd: Not safe for gluten-free or celiac diners. The signature draw is house-made extra-thick wheat noodles (極太手揉み麺), and the tare is a soy-sauce (wheat-based) seasoning over a pork-bone broth. No gluten-free noodles, separate prep, or allergen accommodation is offered or mentioned.
places.vgd: This is a Jiro-style ramen shop built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth with back fat and pork toppings; the bowls are fundamentally pork-based with mounded vegetables on top. No vegan or vegetarian option is offered or mentioned anywhere.

places.chef: abura soba (oil noodle) specialist, second brand of Ichijoji's Bishiya · Kyoto (Ichijoji / Hyakumanben, Sakyo-ku) · Yumin is the abura-soba spin-off of Bishiya (びし屋), a ramen shop in Ichijoji known for drawing lines. The team opened this second, oil-noodle-focused shop in the Hyakumanben student quarter just north of the Hyakumanben crossing near Kyoto University, taking over a space that had been a curry restaurant. Staff from the Ichijoji parent moved over to run it. It opened on October 10, 2025, and was generating buzz before it even opened. · Make oil soba approachable: lighter on the palate than its rich look suggests, with a good balance of acidity and aromatics, and table signage that walks first-timers through how to eat it. Diners mix everything themselves, dial in garlic to taste, and use the counter condiments (vinegar, chili oil, pepper, diced onion) to shift the flavor partway through the bowl. · Abura soba — brothless wheat noodles tossed with an oil-and-tare sauce. Three bowls anchor the menu: the standard abura soba and a spicy version (辛味あぶらそば), both on house-made noodles, plus a 背脂ヤサイあぶらそば (back-fat vegetable) bowl built in a Jiro style on thick, chewy noodles w…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free / not celiac-safe. All bowls use wheat noodles (the regular and spicy abura soba use house-made wheat noodles; the back-fat vegetable bowl uses a thick Jiro-style wheat noodle), and the oil/tare sauce is a typical abura-soba sauce that contains wheat-based soy sauce. There is no gluten-free menu, no separate preparation, and no indication of allergy handling. A celiac diner should avoid this shop.
places.vgd: No vegan option. This is an abura soba (brothless oil noodle) shop whose bowls center on a wheat-based oil/tare sauce, pork fat (背脂), char siu / fatty pork toppings, eggs, and mayo-based extras. The "背脂野菜油そば" (back-fat vegetable) bowl is built on pork fat in a Jiro style. No plant-based bowl is offered; a vegan diner could not be safely accommodated here.
places.hours: 11:00–15:00 / 17:30–22:30 (Friday dinner until 22:00). Sources vary slightly on lunch close (one lists 11:00–14:30). Irregular closures announced on Instagram; some sources note Monday evening closed.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A specialty mazesoba shop that opened on November 20, 2024, on Senbon-dori. The signature dongpo-pork dish is prepared under a Chinese chef who keeps to an authentic recipe while tuning it to Japanese palates.
places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto, Kamigyo-ku (Senbon-Demizu, northwest of Nijo Castle) · A specialty mazesoba shop that opened on November 20, 2024, on Senbon-dori. The signature dongpo-pork dish is prepared under a Chinese chef who keeps to an authentic recipe while tuning it to Japanese palates. · Quality ingredients plus customization: the owner frames the two noodle choices as 'selecting the two ultimate options so you can enjoy Taiwanese mazesoba's deliciousness to the very end,' and sets out 10-plus condiments (garlic vinegar, kombu/anchovy vinegar and more) to encourage mid-meal 味変 (flavor-shifting). · 東坡肉台湾まぜそば — Taiwanese mazesoba crowned with dongpo pork (皮付きの豚の角煮, glossy skin-on braised pork belly slow-cooked with star anise). The house bills itself as Japan's first mazesoba shop that lets you pick your noodle, choosing between a medium-thick full-wheat noodle and a wavy 'wing' noodle so you can enjoy the bowl your way to the last bite.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. No gluten-free noodle, tare, or accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Celiac diners should treat this as unsafe.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The menu centers on pork — signature 東坡肉 (skin-on braised pork belly / dongpo pork), spicy Taiwanese pork mince, chashu rice bowls, and a chicken-paitan ramen. Eggs (味玉) feature prominently. No plant-based bowl is advertised.

This Kakichu branch was opened independently in 1966 (Showa 41) by the fo
places.chef: Seiji Kakichu (founder of this branch; run today by the proprietor couple) · founder, owner-operator · Fukakusa shopping district, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto · Part of the historic Rikimochi (力餅) lineage that began in 1889 in Toyooka as a confectionery and spread across Kansai as a franchise of homey eateries; fewer than about ten of these old shops survive today. This Kakichu branch was opened in 1966 (Showa 41) by Seiji — the father of today's proprietor — under the Rikimochi name, and remains a fixture of the Fukakusa shopping street. · あっさりと飽きのこない家庭的な味 — a light, never-tiring homestyle flavor served in an unpretentious old-fashioned shokudo where everything stays under 1,000 yen and a solo diner is always welcome. · 中華そば (chūka soba) at around 680 yen: a deliberately light, pale broth closer to a gentle udon dashi than a heavy ramen soup, with fine straight noodles, thick-cut char siu, two kinds of kamaboko fish cake, generous Kyoto negi and menma. Their oversized inari sushi (about 150 yen), packed with black sesame, carrot and burdock, is a beloved side.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Showa-era noodle diner. The signature 中華そば uses fine wheat ramen noodles in a dashi-style broth, and the menu is built around wheat-based noodles (udon, soba, chūka soba), rice bowls and inari sushi. There is no indication of gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Broth and tare almost certainly involve wheat-containing soy sauce. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: A meat-and-fish family diner: the 中華そば comes with thick char siu pork, two kinds of fish-cake kamaboko, and a dashi-based broth. Rice bowls and set meals are similarly animal-based. No vegan options are advertised and the kitchen is not set up for plant-based requests.
