rm.bowl: Chuka soba (中華そば) — a crystal-clear duck-forward chukasoba built on a five-bone stock; optionally finished with the table-side trio of pork-and-water-chestnut wontons.

places.notes: Roku is produced by chef Yuji Iwasaki, who earned two Michelin stars at his high-end Chinese restaurant VELROSIER. The shop began as 鴨出汁中華そば ROKU (kamo-dashi / duck-broth chuka-soba) and was renewed and renamed to 中華そば 六 when it reopened on the second floor of GOOD NATURE STATION
places.chef: 岩崎祐司 (Yuji Iwasaki) · owner-chef / producer · Kyoto, Japan — Kawaramachi / Shijo area · Roku is produced by chef Yuji Iwasaki, who earned two Michelin stars at his high-end Chinese restaurant VELROSIER. The shop began as 鴨出汁中華そば ROKU (kamo-dashi / duck-broth chuka-soba) and was renewed and renamed to 中華そば 六 when it reopened on the second floor of GOOD NATURE STATION on May 13, 2023, narrowing its focus to a single, refined Chinese-style noodle soup. · Applying the techniques of fine Chinese cuisine to ramen to create what the shop calls a 唯一無二 (one-of-a-kind) soup — an elevated, restaurant-grade take on the everyday chuka-soba. · The signature 中華そば (Chuka Soba, around ¥1,100): a clear yet deeply layered broth that draws umami from five kinds of bone stock — duck, free-range chicken, venison, beef and pork — and builds further depth with porcini, longan fruit, tomato and dried shiitake. Straight noodles are custom-made to match the clear soup, and hand-made wontons (pork, onion, arrowhead and celery) are added partway through the bowl as a second act.
places.gfd: This is a refined chuka-soba (Chinese-style ramen) specialist. The dish is built on custom-made wheat noodles, almost certainly served with a wheat-based shoyu/Chinese-style tare, and a meat broth drawn from five bone stocks (duck, local chicken, venison, beef, pork). Wonton toppings are wheat-wrapped. No gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or wheat-free option is advertised on any source reviewed. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: The entire concept is centered on an animal broth extracted from five types of bone (duck, free-range chicken, venison, beef, pork), and the signature wontons contain pork. There is no vegetarian or vegan ramen on the menu and no plant-based broth option. Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.
places.hours: Lunch 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:30) / Dinner 18:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Closes early when the broth runs out.

The building once housed a Japanese restaurant; its high ceilings and shoes-off, eel's-nest layout — a few tables by the entrance an
places.chef: owner · 中華 六六 sits in a renovated Kyoto machiya just west of the Horikawa-Kitaoji crossing, in the Murasakino district a short walk from Daitoku-ji temple. Its high ceilings and shoes-off, eel's-nest layout — a few tables by the entrance and a long counter deep in the back — make a warm, retro setting for Chinese home-style cooking that locals treat as a townhouse take on neighborhood Chinese. · A neighborhood kitchen that prizes authentic ingredients — its dried tofu is specially sourced from mainland China — and leans on volume and comfort over flash, the sort of filling, hospitable lunch that keeps regulars coming back. · The kitchen is known for hearty, generous lunch sets around 1,000 yen — a fried-chicken (yurin-chi) set, mapo and weekly-rotating set menus — alongside a soy-sauce chuka-soba. That bowl leads with a clean shoyu base carrying a gentle tang and the sweetness of scallion and onion, medium straight noodles, a thick slab of char siu, and menma that one local guide called the best they had ever eaten.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. The signature chuka-soba uses standard wheat ramen noodles in a soy-sauce (醤油) broth, and the wider menu (gyoza, fried chicken/karaage, shumai, stir-fries) leans heavily on wheat flour and wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free menu, no celiac accommodation, and no allergen handling is advertised.

rm.bowl: Tori paitan ramen, shio version (the salt tare best showcases the chicken umami, finished with lemon); the night-only Taiwan mazesoba is the other house specialty.

places.notes: This is the original flagship (一号店) of Kirameki no Tori, opened in 2013 near the Kawaramachi-Marutamachi crossing in Kyoto's Kamigyo ward. From this single counter the brand grew into a chicken-focused group (operated by Kirameki no Mirai Co.) with around two dozen shops across K
places.chef: flagship ramen shop, chain origin store · Kyoto (Kamigyo-ku, near the Imperial Palace) · This is the original flagship (一号店) of Kirameki no Tori, opened in 2013 just north of the Kawaramachi-Marutamachi crossing (Demizu-cho, Kamigyo ward) in Kyoto. From this single counter the brand grew into a chicken-focused group (operated by Kirameki no Mirai Co.) with around 30 shops across Kyoto, Osaka, Shiga and Nara, plus a noodle workshop in Nishikyo ward — but the Demizu-cho shop remains where it all started. · Everything revolves around the chicken: the broth is built from chicken bones simmered with thigh meat and skin for a rich, sweet umami that is full-bodied without being heavy, and the noodles are made in-house from 100% Hokkaido wheat for a fragrant, crisp bite. The group's stated aim is to keep taste and service at a high level even as it expands. · Tori-paitan ramen — a creamy chicken white-broth bowl offered in shio, shoyu and miso. The signature shio version is finished with chicken-thigh chashu, white leek, mizuna, thread chili, menma and a slice of lemon for brightness. Taiwan mazesoba and karaage round out the menu.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. The ramen is built on in-house wheat noodles (made from 100% Hokkaido wheat at the group's own noodle workshop), and the menu also features Taiwan mazesoba (wheat) and karaage (wheat-dredged fried chicken). The chicken-paitan broth comes in shio/shoyu/miso tares; the shoyu and miso versions involve wheat-based soy sauce/miso. There is no published gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergen-handling information. A celiac diner should not eat here.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The entire concept is chicken: the broth is a chicken-bone paitan simmered with chicken thigh meat and skin, toppings include chicken-thigh chashu, and the shop is paired with karaage. No vegetable or plant-based broth or noodle option is published.
places.hours: 11:00–15:00 (last order 14:30) / 18:00–23:00 (last order 22:30). Open daily, with occasional temporary closures.

places.chef: neighborhood Chinese diner, ramen / 中華そば shop · Kyoto (Kitaoji-Omiya, Kamigyo Ward) · 御旅飯店 is a long-standing neighborhood Chinese diner (町中華) tucked into the old Kitaoji-Omiya quarter near Funaokayama and the Daitokuji temple precinct. Its name comes from the adjacent 御旅所 (otabi-sho) — the resting place for the portable shrine during Imamiya Shrine's festival each May. This pocket of the city flourished as a merchant district in the Edo period and quieted after the early Showa era as the Nishijin textile trade declined, leaving behind exactly the kind of unhurried local shop the restaurant still embodies. · Hearty, affordable, community-first cooking — big portions, free rice refills, and a deep two-sided menu of Chinese standards (fried rice, gyoza, noodles, fried and grilled dishes) priced for everyday eating. · The house pride is the 御旅丼 (Otabi-don), a local bowl that is, in the words of one writer, 'barely known outside the neighborhood': stir-fried pork with cabbage, carrot, onion, wood-ear mushroom and egg, bound in a Chinese-style sauce over a generous mound of rice (said to hold roughly three servings). The shop carries on the lineage of the so-called 'phantom Iwakura ramen' (幻の岩倉ラーメン), a Kyoto street-cart ramen whose flavor passed to Yamasan Ramen before that shop e
places.chef: Iicho (proprietor) · owner, chef · Kyoto (Iwakura / Shimogamo lineage) · Iicho opened in 1998 in the Shimogamo neighborhood of Sakyo-ku, a short walk east of Kitaoji across the Kamogawa. The shop carries on the lineage of the so-called 'phantom Iwakura ramen' (幻の岩倉ラーメン), a Kyoto street-cart ramen whose flavor passed to Yamasan Ramen before that shop eventually moved away to Shiga; the founder learned the style from that tradition and brought it into the modern era. · The proprietor sums up his approach as 'people are moved by heart,' treating each day's open as the start of a fresh battle and refining the bowl through constant, patient improvement. · An assari shoyu chuka-soba: a lightly cloudy broth of chicken bone (specifically the shin) and pork bone in roughly a 7:3 ratio, finished with back fat, thin chashu, and Kyoto negi. The tare is Sawai shoyu, a twice-fermented 'double-koji' soy sauce that gives the bowl its punchy backbone. Medium-thin straight noodles from Rairaiken keep an old-Showa chuka-soba character. The egg-and-pork-fat yakimeshi, with heavily caramelized edges, is a beloved companion.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles (from Rairaiken/Kairaikian seimen) and a wheat-based soy sauce tare (Sawai twice-fermented "double-koji" shoyu), with no gluten-free menu or allergen accommodation noted anywhere. Treat as off-limits for strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian friendly. The signature broth is a chicken-bone and pork-bone blend (roughly 7:3) with back fat and sliced chashu pork; the popular yakimeshi side uses egg and pork fat. No plant-based option is offered.

places.chef: ラーメン店, まぜそば専門 · Fushimi-Fukakusa, Kyoto, near Fujinomori Station · 麺屋 誉 (Menya Homare) opened on October 22, 2025 as the reborn version of a neighborhood favorite, フカクサ製麺食堂 (Fukakusa Seimen Shokudo). That predecessor began life humbly as a mazesoba specialist tucked into the corner of a parking lot, later moved into a proper storefront, and built a following on chicken-paitan (鶏白湯) ramen. places.chef: tantan-men specialist, counter-only neighborhood shop · A long-running, much-loved tantan-men specialist tucked into a small storefront on Shijo-dori, in the Mibu quarter of Kyoto's Nakagyo Ward between Shijo-Omiya and Saiin. places.chef: independent ramen shop · Kyoto (Saiin / 右京区) · A long-running independent ramen counter in Kyoto's Saiin district, near Saikyogoku, that has been a fixture of the Saiin-Katsura ramen scene long enough to outlast its own name. places.chef: Sai (さい) · owner, chef · Kyoto ramen lineage (Ichijoji's Takayasu) · The owner-chef, known as Sai-san, spent about 15 years making ramen at Takayasu (高安), the famous, perennially queued shop on Ichijoji's 'Ramen Street' in Kyoto. places.chef: owner-operator · Fushimi, Kyoto · A small owner-run counter shop tucked near Fushimi Station, beneath the Kintetsu rail overpass in the Fukakusa area of Fushimi. The owner trained at earlier ramen shops (known locally as Dainaka and Gankokumen) before going independent and opening Tanukiya around 2015-2016; it has since grown into one of the most loved ramen stops in the Fushimi neighborhood, reaching roughly its 10th year in 2025. · Big, satisfying, unabashedly rich bowls done in a tiny nine-seat space, with broth given time to mature rather than rushed. · Two faces define the shop. By day and night it pours an aged tonkotsu ramen made by simmering pork bones over high heat for hours and then resting the broth to deepen its umami into a thick, almost porridge-like richness, served over chewy medium-thick straight noodles and limited to about 20 bowls per service. Its other headline is the mazesoba: extra-thick noodles coated in a punchy tare with thick slabs of chashu and a heap of garlic. A genuinely full-sized house fried rice (chahan) rounds out the order and is a destination in its own right.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (Fushimi), in the Meimon ramen lineage · Henteko is a tiny ramen counter tucked down a narrow alley in the Fukakusa/Sumizome area of Fushimi (near Sumizome Station / Fujimori Shrine), opened around 2019 and reopened after a renovation in 2024 that expanded its original six-seat counter with a couple of tables. The owner trained at Meimon (名門), the Kyoto establishment often called the founder of the city's rich tonkotsu style, and he carries that grounding into his own shop while constantly tinkering with new ideas. · A minimalist, quality-first operation: a small counter, a carefully simmered chicken broth, and straightforward bowls rather than fuss, paired with a steady stream of playful limited specials. · The house bowl is the Henteko Shoyu: a creamy chicken-paitan broth married to a soy tare, topped with a few thick slices of chashu, tender menma, and medium-thick noodles with a firm bite. places.chef: owner-chef · Nishijin, Kyoto (Kamigyo-ku), on Senbon-dori · A genuine Showa-era town-Chinese shop that has fed the Nishijin neighborhood for some 40 years, dating back to when the Senbon district was a buzzing entertainment quarter known as 'Kawaramachi in the east, Senbon in the west' (東の河原町、西の千本), with locals out for an evening stroll. As the surrounding district quieted over the decades, the shop stayed busy and beloved. · Hearty, no-frills Nagasaki-style Chinese cooking done the same honest way for decades — generous portions, a hot wok, and a welcoming counter for solo diners. · Nagasaki champon and Nagasaki sara-udon — the house signatures. The champon is a milky, umami-rich broth piled with chewy noodles, pork, shrimp, squid, fishcake (kamaboko/chikuwa), cabbage, bean sprouts and carrot; the sara-udon layers ultra-thin crispy fried noodles under a glossy, vegetable-and-seafood gravy. It is run as an intimate husband-and-wife operation with just fourteen seats split between a counte
places.chef: owner-chef (husband-and-wife operation) · Narukami is a small, family-run chuka-soba and gyoza specialist tucked along Senbon-dori in Kyoto's Kamigyo ward, a short walk from the Kitano-Hakubaicho area near Kitano Tenmangu. It is run as an intimate husband-and-wife operation with just fourteen seats split between a counter and a couple of tables. · The kitchen leans on chicken bones alone, slowly drawn out, aiming for a broth with real depth that is still approachable enough to eat every day rather than a one-time heavy hit. · The signature bowl is a classic Kyoto-style chuka soba: a broth built from carefully selected chicken bones simmered patiently (鶏ガラ100%), finished with a scattering of back fat (背脂) over a soy tare. Despite its rich, glistening look it drinks surprisingly light and clean, with a hidden touch of ichimi togarashi for lift, served over medium straight noodles with chashu. Alongside the ramen, the shop is known for its gyoza and a popular ebimeshi (shrimp fried rice).
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. There is no indication of gluten-free preparation, no dedicated equipment, and no allergen accommodation noted. Not safe for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The signature broth is made from chicken bones (鶏ガラ100%) finished with scattered back fat (背脂), topped with chashu pork; gyoza typically contain pork. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen offerings.

rm.bowl: The house is famous for its year-round cold noodles (reimen), but the hot bowl to order is the chuka-soba — a Kyoto-style pork-bone-and-chicken shoyu ramen; chashu-men adds extra roast pork.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Misonobashi Sakai traces back to a Sakai family Chinese kitchen founded in Kyoto's Kita ward in the prewar/early-Showa era; this branch opened in 1982 as an independent offshoot of the original 'Chuka no Sakai' near Daitokuji, settling by the Misonobashi bridge toward Kamigamo.
places.chef: family-run Chinese noodle shop · Kyoto, Kita-ku · Misonobashi Sakai traces back to a Sakai family Chinese kitchen founded in Kyoto's Kita ward in the prewar/early-Showa era; this branch opened in 1982 as an independent offshoot of the original 'Chuka no Sakai' near Daitokuji, settling by the Misonobashi bridge toward Kamigamo. · A neighborhood institution built on one perfected dish, served year-round — captured in the local saying that when you think cold noodles you think Sakai, and when you think Sakai you think cold noodles. · Sesame-sauce cold noodles — the 焼豚冷麺 (roast-pork cold noodles): plump, chewy thick noodles bound in a thick, emulsified pale-yellow sesame dare that balances sweetness, tang, and a mustard kick, finished with sliced roast pork; a ham version is also offered.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation. The house specialty is cold noodles (冷麺) made with thick wheat ("ムチムチ太麺") noodles, and the menu centers on Chinese noodle dishes (中華そば) — all wheat-based. There is no published allergen or gluten-free information. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The flagship bowls are 焼豚冷麺 (roast-pork cold noodles) and ham cold noodles, and the kitchen is a Chinese-cuisine shop built around pork. The sesame dare and other dishes have no stated plant-based versions, and no vegetarian/vegan menu is advertised.

places.chef: Morikawa Ryohei (森川良平) · owner, chef, founder · 京都市左京区・岡崎（平安神宮の北東） · A craftsman ramen shop born from a yatai (hand-pushed food cart). Founder Ryohei Morikawa, originally from Ishikawa Prefecture, had worked as a materials dealer and a taxi driver before learning to make ramen by volunteering unpaid for five months — late nights after his own shift work — at a shop called Homin (芳眠) in Kamikatsura. In 1972 he began pushing a hinoki-wood cart along Marutamachi-dori in Okazaki, opening each evening around the time the first star appeared, which gave the shop its name, Ichibanboshi ("first star"). After about three years he took over a brick-walled space left by a closing nearby steakhouse and put down permanent roots; the ivy-covered, café-like brick exterior near Heian Shrine is now the local landmark. · Morikawa credits his customers for the recipe itself: "お客さんのほうがラーメンにくわしいんです。こだわりのあるお客さんのアドバイスをたくさん取り入れて、今の味になりました" — "Customers know ramen better than I do; I took in a lot of advice from discerning regulars, and that's how today's flavor came to be." He says the taste evolved over the years alongside the regulars who eat it. · A single bowl: chuka-soba. A clear (seiyu) broth of po…

The only side is white rice, and the house-made pickles served with the bowl could in theory be safe, but the shop offers no allergen information and the kitchen handles w…

places.chef: owner-operator · Mototanaka, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto · Jiei opened in February 2016 in a quiet residential pocket of Mototanaka in Sakyo Ward, about five minutes' walk from Mototanaka Station and just north of Kyoto University's agriculture campus, taking over a small storefront that earlier housed a Western-style (yoshoku) restaurant called Kitchen Gorilla. Now approaching its tenth year, it has become a low-key neighborhood fixture rather than a tourist destination. · Do one bowl, and do it carefully. The taciturn owner is described as working quietly and methodically, plating a nostalgic, old-fashioned (昔ながらの) Kyoto ramen meant to feel homely and warming rather than flashy. · A single classic Kyoto-style chukasoba (中華そば) in a style that reviewers liken to the Takara-ya (宝屋) / Taiei (大栄) Kyoto-ramen tradition: a tea-colored tonkotsu-shoyu broth with mellow, comforting umami, served over medium-thin straight noodles and topped with thick-cut pork-belly chashu, menma (bamboo shoots) and freshly hand-cut scallions. Offered as regular or large, plus a chashu version; rice rounds out the short menu.

Not suitable for celiac diners. No GF information is published anywhere.

places.chef: Operated by 五辻の昆布 (Itutuji no Konbu) · Kyoto, in the Kitano-Hakubaicho / Kitano Tenmangu district of Kamigyo-ku. · Kiichi is the ramen room of Itutuji no Konbu, a Kyoto kombu specialist founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) on Nishi-Itsutsuji in Kamigyo-ku. The ramen counter sits on the second floor above the family's historic kelp shop, near Kitano Tenmangu. · The shop exists to help people rediscover the value of kombu: 昆布専門店が『昆布の価値を再認識してもらう』ために作った『昆布らぁめん』 — a kombu specialist's answer to falling kelp consumption and changing kitchens. · The signature 昆布らぁめん (kombu ramen) is built on a broth blending ma-kombu, rausu and rishiri kelp, lifted with bonito and seafood (squid and shellfish) and — unusually for ramen — made with no meat stock. places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto (Takano / Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku) · Ramen Viska opened on July 14, 2023, in a quiet residential pocket behind Takano Post Office, on the fringe of Ichijoji's famously crowded ramen battleground. It is a true one-person shop: the owner cooks, serves, and chats single-handedly. The space is a renovated former snack bar with a glossy high bar-style counter of about five seats, and the owner greets guests in a suit and tie rather than the usual ramen-cook garb. There is no noren curtain out front. · A minimalist, single-minded devotion to tonkotsu done well — quality broth over a broad menu, served personally and explained in detail to anyone curious. · Super-rich kotteri tonkotsu: a pork-bone broth simmered until thick enough that, as locals joke, the spoon could stand up in it, yet it stays mild and clean on the palate with no porky funk, drinking almost like a potage. The lineup is deliberately spare — kotteri (rich), assari (a remarkably clear, transparent tonkotsu, finished with yuzu zest), a Bisuro (ビス郎) bowl, and tsukemen — paired with medium-straight noodles and well-seasoned roast-pork chashu. places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle tonkotsu shop with no gluten-free offering. The noodles are wheat, the tare is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu, and the menu (kotteri/assari/tsukemen) is built around standard ramen components. places.vgd: Every bowl is built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth and topped with roast-pork chashu; there is no vegetable or vegan broth and no meat-free option on the menu. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto (originally Uzumasa / west Kyoto) · Sugichiyo is the revival of a legendary Kyoto ramen shop. The original opened in 1999 in the Uzumasa area of western Kyoto and drew daily lines for roughly a decade before it closed at the end of 2009 — reportedly because the crowds it attracted had become difficult to sustain. After about twelve years dormant, the name returned in June 2021 in a renovated spot down a Takase River alley just west of Shijo-Kawaramachi, in the heart of central Kyoto's nightlife district. The current team is said to have inherited the complete original recipe directly from the founder. · Faithfully carry forward a beloved recipe rather than reinvent it — a nostalgic, unpretentious bowl served with quiet, courteous hospitality instead of the high-intensity style of many modern ramen shops. · Chashu ramen — the bowl that built the shop's reputation. The pork-bone soy-sauce broth carries the deep richness of Kyoto-style ramen with a thin veil of back fat on top, yet drinks lighter and cleaner than its color suggests; the soy tare is comparatively restrained, letting the broth's umami lead. It sits, almost unexpectedly, in a quiet residential pocket of Matsugasaki near the ward office, drawing queues to a converted white single-family house with sunlit counter seating and a breezy balcony area. · Rather than the heavier bowls Kyoto is often known for, the shop leans on technique and restraint, using the whipped-foam broth and carefully drawn dashi to keep flavors smooth and the finish clean. · The house bowl is the 泡白湯 (awa paitan): a broth simmered from whole chicken and chicken bones, then whipped into a creamy, mousse-like foam and finished with a Japanese-style soy tare for a surprisingly clean, light aftertaste. The kitchen also offers a chicken paitan, a fish-soy (gyokai-shoyu) ramen built on a low-temperature dashi of three fish flakes, kombu and dried shiitake with chicken oil, and a rich fish-pork tsukemen.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free and not suitable for celiacs. places.chef: owner-chef · 京都市下京区 七条大宮・梅小路 · A small, time-worn ramen counter tucked into the Shichijo-Omiya block near Umekoji Park and Umekoji-Kyoto-Nishi Station. It belongs to Kyoto's beloved 'Akira-kei' (旭系) lineage — the nostalgic Kyoto soy-sauce ramen tradition associated with the famous Daiichi-Asahi. The owner is said to have trained at a shop called Taiki before opening his own counter, and the place has the lived-in, slightly aged storefront of a long-standing local fixture. · A taciturn owner with a quiet, single-minded devotion to ramen — no frills, no trend-chasing, just an honest bowl in the old Kyoto idiom. Regulars describe the flavor as deeply nostalgic, evoking long-gone neighborhood shops. · Kyoto-style shoyu ramen — a clear, pork-forward broth where the pig's umami and richness are balanced against a restrained soy edge, served over soft medium-thick straight noodles that soak up the broth, finished with loin chashu, a generous pile of scallions and bean sprouts. A miso version and a notably good spicy miso are also offered.
places.gfd: This is a classic Kyoto-style soy-sauce ramen shop. Not suitable for celiacs. The only other listed item is gyoza (wheat wrappers). Assume cross-contamination throughout a single shared kitchen.
places.vgd: The menu is limited to shoyu and miso ramen built on a pork-based (旭系) broth with chashu pork, plus gyoza. There are no vegan or vegetarian options and no plant-based broth. Not a vegan-friendly destination.

places.chef: proprietor (女将) — Miyazaki family · Kyoto (Shijo-Omiya / Nakagyo Ward) · Founded in 1948 (Showa 23) at Shijo-Omiya, Kyoichi Honten has anchored the same corner for over 75 years. The shop began life as a zenzai (sweet red-bean) shop before becoming the bustling everyday diner it is today; the current building was rebuilt in 1976 but keeps its retro, time-capsule feel. It is run by the Miyazaki family, with a hands-on female proprietor who happily steers customers toward her favorite pairings. · The shop's long-standing motto is 'umai, hayai, yasui' — delicious, fast, and cheap — the creed of a true neighborhood diner serving locals, laborers and students alike. · Curry chuka soba (カレー中華) — Chinese wheat noodles buried under a glossy, spicy-sweet curry an (sauce) built from a long-simmered broth, multiple curry rouxs and secret seasonings, finished with braised wagyu beef for depth. places.chef: independent neighborhood Chinese / noodle house, keeper of the 鳳舞系 からしそば tradition · Kyoto (北区 紫野, on Horikawa near Kitaoji) · 鳳飛 is part of Kyoto's celebrated 鳳舞系 — the lineage of Chinese cooks who trained under master 高華吉, a Cantonese immigrant, at the legendary 鳳舞, which opened in 1967 and closed, much mourned, in 2009. 高 is remembered as a pioneer of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking who reworked Chinese food for local palates into something light, restrained and broth-forward — chicken- and kombu-based, with the oil and aggressive aromatics pulled back. Disciples who struck out on their own carried the 鳳 (phoenix) character of 鳳舞 into their own shop names; 鳳飛 is regarded as a direct heir of that tradition. (The lineage is sometimes traced further back through 高's earlier restaurants 第一樓 and 飛雲, and ultimately the Taisho-era 支那料理ハマムラ.) · Gentle, unshowy, deeply Kyoto: minimal oil, no aggressive aromatics, prices kept low enough for neighbors to eat here regularly — Chinese food rebuilt as everyday comfort food rather than a feast. · からしそば — a noodle dish found essentially only at 鳳舞系 shops: boiled Chinese noodles tossed with mustard and bound in a lightly sweet, glossy chicken-and-k…
places.gfd: The headline dishes here are wheat-noodle plates — からしそば (mustard noodles) and 中華そば — served with house-made wheat noodles, and the kitchen leans on soy-based seasonings. Spring rolls, shumai, gyoza and fried noodles are all wheat-based as well. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation, so this is not a safe choice for celiacs.
places.vgd: This is a meat-and-seafood Chinese kitchen: the からしそば is built on chicken and shrimp, signature plates include からし鶏 (fried chicken), juicy pork shumai, and 酢豚 (sweet-and-sour pork), and broths/stir-fries rely on animal stock. No vegan menu or dedicated plant-based options are advertised; a vegan diner would have very little to eat.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Nabura was opened on 8 August 2022 by a chef who spent about 35 years cooking traditional Kyoto-style Japanese cuisine (kappo/washoku) before turning that craft to ramen, in the Kitano Tenmangu / Kamishichiken area of Kamigyo-ku.
places.chef: owner-chef · The owner is a keen fishing enthusiast, and the shop name 'Nabura' refers to a school of small fish leaping at the sea surface as they are chased by larger fish - a fisherman's sign of opportunity and good fortune. The name was suggested by a fishing-loving staff member, and the staff wear Nabura T-shirts as a maritime good-luck symbol. · Nabura was opened on 8 August 2022 by a chef who spent about 35 years cooking traditional Kyoto-style Japanese cuisine (kappo/washoku) before turning that craft to ramen, in the Kitano Tenmangu / Kamishichiken area of Kamigyo-ku. · The shop deliberately keeps salt low and the broth clean and digestible so that anyone, regardless of age or gender, can eat it as an everyday meal - the owner says you can finish all the soup and still feel light afterward (誰でも美味しく食べられる). · The signature bowl is a completely additive-free (無化調) ramen whose broth is drawn only from kombu (kelp) and saba (mackerel) - no fish powder, no chemical seasoning - finished with a piece of fried mackerel tatsuta-age floating in the soup. Tsukemen is also a mainstay, including a rich seafood dipping broth.

places.chef: independent ramen shop · Kyoto (Kita-Shirakawa, Sakyo Ward) · Ramen Akatsuki is a long-running neighborhood ramen-ya in Kyoto's Kita-Shirakawa quarter of Sakyo Ward, a stone's throw from the Kitashirakawa-kōmae city-bus stop and within walking distance of Mototanaka Station. Reports describe it as approaching its 30th year in business — a genuine local fixture rather than a trend shop. It runs from late morning straight through to around 3:00 a.m. every day, making it a dependable late-night bowl for students and locals alike. · A straightforward, satisfying bowl that lets a clean pork-and-chicken broth and generous back-fat do the talking — comfort-food Kyoto ramen built for everyday, all-hours eating. · A Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu ramen built on a long-simmered pork-and-chicken broth finished with a Japanese-dashi soy tare and crowned with a scattering of sweet back-fat. Despite the rich-looking, glistening surface, the soup drinks surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy off-notes. The thick, tender braised char siu is treated as a star in its own right, and regulars are pointed toward extra char siu or the loaded 'Akatsuki Special.'

places.chef: ramen shop · Kyoto (Fushimi-Momoyama) · A Fushimi institution tucked beneath the elevated railway tracks right outside Kintetsu Momoyamagoryomae Station, Daichu has been serving its rich tonkotsu since opening in 1995. The narrow, corridor-shaped space — counter up front, tables behind — keeps a nostalgic Showa-era atmosphere, marked from the street by a yellow signboard and a big red lantern. In a district full of izakaya, it runs from late morning until around 2:00 a.m. daily, drawing a steady stream of locals from lunch through late night. · The kitchen prides itself on a flavor 'you can't get at a chain' — breaking the bones in-house and simmering large batches of pork and chicken bones for a full 24 hours rather than reconstituting a pre-made base. places.chef: owner-operator ramen counter · Kyoto, Japan — a neighborhood町中華 (town-Chinese / local ramen) shop serving the surrounding residents and after-work salarymen. · Open since 1993, Shomen is a small, well-worn ramen counter tucked into the Horikawa Shopping Street on the west side of Horikawa-dori, a short walk toward Marutamachi and Imadegawa. It belongs to the Kyoto back-fat shoyu tradition that traces back to the famous Masutani style — a lineage some regulars argue Shomen executes even better than the original. · An almost obsessive devotion to the back fat — the fat is sourced from Kyushu — so that the rich, collagen-laced sheen on the surface is the defining character of the bowl rather than an afterthought. · Chuka soba: thin, straight noodles in a chicken-bone (鶏ガラ) broth finished with a glistening layer of pork back fat (背脂) and an aged soy-sauce tare, topped with chashu braised until meltingly tender (とろとろ) and firm menma. A bowl runs about ¥650; the ramen-and-fried-rice set about ¥850.

places.vgd: Not a vegan-friendly option. The signature and essentially only style is a chicken-bone broth enriched with pork back fat and topped with braised pork chashu, so the broth, fat and toppings are all animal-derived and there is no plant-based ramen on the menu.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A newcomer to Kyoto's ramen scene, Menya Ichimen Senshin opened in March 2024 in a roomy former eatery space in Kamigyo Ward, a short walk northwest toward Nijo Castle. The name carries the spirit of devoting oneself wholeheartedly to a single bowl of noodles.
places.chef: independent ramen shop · Kyoto (Kamigyo-ku, Senbon-Marutamachi) · A newcomer to Kyoto's ramen scene, Menya Ichimen Senshin opened on 9 March 2024 in a roomy former eatery space in Kamigyo Ward, a short walk northwest toward Nijo Castle. Alongside it is a chicken paitan (tori-paitan) and a special shoyu ramen priced at just 700 yen.

places.chef: owner · Ramen Yucho opened on 18 February 2025 on the second floor of the Iidaya Building, a short walk from Kyoto-Kawaramachi Station in the busy Shijo-Kawaramachi quarter. Styled as a tucked-away hidden-gem shop with a clean, modern Japanese interior and a U-shaped counter, it set out to do one thing well in a city where ginger-forward ramen is genuinely uncommon. · A focused, single-bowl shop: pour everything into one warming, refined ginger soy-sauce ramen rather than a long menu, with broth and ginger meant to leave you physically warmed from the inside. · The signature and essentially only dish is the Kyoto ginger soy-sauce ramen. A crystal-clear seafood broth is drawn from three kinds of fish dashi (horse mackerel, mackerel and bonito), then driven by ginger both dissolved in the soup and laid on top as fresh needle-cut strips. It is served with thin, supple straight noodles from the Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teikoku, and topped with chashu pork, roast beef, naruto, Kujo green onion, menma and spinach. Diners choose Single, Double or Triple by the number of chashu and roast-beef slices, and a side of ginger dashi rice is also offered.
places.gfd: Specialist ginger soy-sauce ramen shop. The single menu item is built on wheat noodles (from Menya Teikoku) in a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that is normally wheat-based, over a fish/dashi broth (horse mackerel, bonito, mackerel). No gluten-free noodle or tare option and no indication of allergen accommodation, so not safe for celiacs. Anyone strictly avoiding gluten should not eat here.
places.vgd: The bowl is fundamentally a fish/dashi-based broth (horse mackerel, mackerel and bonito stock) topped with chashu pork and roast beef. Not vegetarian or vegan, and there are no plant-based options on the menu, which serves only the ginger soy-sauce ramen.

places.chef: owner-operator, successor (founder's younger brother carrying on the recipe) · Kyoto · Shinshintei is widely credited as the birthplace of Kyoto-style white miso ramen. The lineage began as a humble food stall around 1960 and grew into a brick-and-mortar shop opened in 1972 in the Fushacho area of central Kyoto. Over nearly four decades it built a devoted following before the original first-generation owner retired and closed that location in 2009 due to age. Rather than let the recipe disappear, the founder's younger brother inherited the name and the noren and reopened the shop in the Ichijoji district, where it carries the tradition forward today as a lunch-only neighborhood institution. · Keep the original white-miso recipe alive and unchanged - a mellow, comforting, deeply flavored bowl made the same way it has been for decades, served simply at lunch. · The signature bowl is white miso ramen (白味噌ラーメン) - a gentle, mellow, slightly sweet white-miso broth that is distinct from the heartier Sapporo style. It pairs a concentrated dashi with a light white miso (淡めの白味噌), is piled with plenty of vegetables, and is served with straight Kyoto-style noodles that meet the smooth broth.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop whose signature is white miso ramen; miso tare and the broth setup mean wheat is integral, and there is no published gluten-free option or dedicated handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The ramen is built on dashi and pork/meat elements with chashu and other meat toppings, and no vegan or vegetarian bowl is advertised. Plant-only diners cannot reliably be accommodated here.

places.chef: 寺田育弘 (Terada Yasuhiro) · owner, chef · Kyoto-style Chinese (京都中華), Cantonese-rooted but refined and lightly seasoned, in the 鳳舞 (Houmai) / 第一樓 (Daiichiro) lineage. · 龍鳳 is a small, unpretentious Kyoto town-Chinese counter tucked into the Rokkaku lane just off the Shinkyogoku arcade, where it has operated for decades. Its proprietor, Terada Yasuhiro, trained under two pillars of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking — 第一樓 (Daiichiro), the postwar restaurant opened around 1951, and the legendary 鳳舞 (Houmai), widely regarded as the fountainhead of 京都中華. He worked as a skilled chef at both before opening his own shop, carrying forward that lineage alongside sister-spirit establishments like 鳳泉. · Faithful preservation of the original Daiichiro recipe and taste. The dish was born as a course finale at Daiichiro because it travelled to the table more easily than soup noodles; Terada keeps that heritage intact while cooking his version longer to deepen the broth's umami, and historically swapping in seasonal ingredients (matsutake for shiitake in season, fresh bamboo shoots over canned). · からしそば (karashi soba) — straight noodles pre-coated with mustard paste under a gentle, mildly sweet soy-based …

places.chef: tonkotsu ramen specialist · Ichijoji, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · Kyomenya opened on December 12, 2016 along Ichijoji's famously competitive ramen street in Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, near the well-known Ramen Yokozuna. It carved out its niche by going against the grain: while Ichijoji leans toward lighter chicken-based broths, Kyomenya planted its flag on unapologetically heavy, ultra-rich tonkotsu. · The aim is a broth that is intensely rich and creamy — dorodoro thick — yet kept smooth and balanced rather than merely heavy (濃厚ですがくどさはありません), with the pork bone simmered long and combined with seafood stock for depth. · The flagship bowl is the Kyo-no Tonkotsu (驚濃とんこつ) — a viscous, cream-thick pork-bone broth rounded out with seafood dashi, using roughly three times the pork bone of an ordinary tonkotsu ramen (通常の豚骨ラーメンの約3倍). The lineup also includes the Mega Tonkotsu (メガとんこつ, water and pork bones only, simmered for hours), a chicken-enriched Tori Tonkotsu (驚濃とりとんこつ), a milder Maroyaka Tonkotsu (まろやかとんこつ), and mazesoba.
places.gfd: This is a tonkotsu ramen specialist: wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth, with the usual ramen tare. No gluten-free options are offered and there is no indication of allergy accommodation. Not suitable for celiac diners.

places.chef: owner · Yokohama, Japan · Saitoya is a Yokohama iekei ramen shop whose owner trained at Tagamiya (田上家), a respected Yokohama family-ramen house founded in 2014, and whose lineage traces back to Yoshimuraya (吉村家), the founding shop of the entire iekei genre. The original Saitoya opened in Yokohama's Negishi district in August 2022; this Ichijoji shop, opened July 27, 2024, is the third Saitoya location and the brand's first venture into the Kansai region. · The owner brews the broth in-house and embraces the iekei idea that the bowl naturally shifts through the day — the flavor you get at the lunch opening differs from the late-evening pour, which they treat as a feature of honest, freshly-simmered cooking rather than a flaw. · Chashu-men: a rich tonkotsu-and-chicken-oil broth with a soy-based tare, served over Sakai Seimen noodles and topped with tender smoked pork chashu, spinach, nori seaweed, and egg. Diners can customize noodle firmness, oil level, and tare strength in classic iekei fashion, and add cabbage or white negi the Yokohama way.

There is no gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no indication of allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners. Rice bowls are available as sides but are prepared in the same kitchen alongside wheat ramen.
places.vgd: The entire concept is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken-oil broth with chashu pork, egg, and a soy-sauce tare. There are no vegetarian or vegan ramen options. places.chef: owner-chef · Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto · 本気つけ麺山下 opened on May 25, 2026 in the heart of Ichijoji, the neighborhood widely regarded as Kyoto's most fiercely competitive ramen district. It took over the space of the well-loved shop "Tsurukame Ichijoji," which closed at the end of March 2026, refreshing the storefront into a clean, bright counter room of eight seats. The proprietor is understood to have trained at a well-known ramen establishment before striking out on his own here. · The shop keeps its focus deliberately narrow, offering only its two tsukemen and letting the noodles and dip do the talking, with a stated wish to become a place loved by many. · A two-bowl tsukemen specialist. The signature 魚介醤油つけ麺 pairs thick, springy noodles with a concentrated bonito-and-dried-sardine fish broth balanced by an aromatic soy tare. The second pillar, 胡麻豆乳担々つけ麺, folds rich roasted sesame and creamy soy milk into a tantan dip crowned with meat-miso for a richness-meets-balance bowl.
places.gfd: No gluten-free option. This is a dedicated tsukemen specialist: both bowls are built on wheat noodles (described as thick, whole-grain-flour-containing noodles) dipped in a soy-sauce-based fish broth (gyokai shoyu) or a sesame-soy-milk tantan broth, both of which use wheat-based soy sauce tare. The wheat noodles plus wheat shoyu mean neither bowl is safe for celiac or gluten-sensitive diners, and no gluten-free preparation is offered or mentioned anywhere.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The fish-soy tsukemen broth is made from bonito (katsuo) and dried sardines (niboshi/iriko), and the sesame-soy-milk tantan bowl is topped with meat-miso (niku-miso); both are animal-based. Although the tantan broth uses soy milk (tonyu), it is not a vegan preparation. No vegan or vegetarian option is offered.

places.chef: 帯刀（店主） · owner, chef · Kyoto (Murasakino / Kitano area) · Owner-chef who trained at 猪一 (Inoichi), a Michelin-recognized Kyoto dashi-soba/ramen establishment, before opening Menya Rennosuke in April 2023 in a renovated traditional wooden house tucked into a quiet Murasakino residential alley. · The chef set out to 'ラーメン屋というイメージを払拭したかった' — to dispel the everyday image of a ramen shop — pursuing refined, additive-free (無化調; no chemical seasoning) cooking that expresses Kyoto's water and terroir, served in a minimalist, jazz-scored space with Kiyomizu-ware bowls. He also plans seasonal evolution such as cold noodles in summer. · らぁ麺 — a delicate clear seafood-dashi bowl. The broth is 100% fish-based, built from two kinds of kombu and Ibuki iriko (dried sardines) layered with saba, urume and katsuo bushi, with no animal stock at all. House-made straight noodles use Kyoto 'Setokirara' wheat with Inner Mongolian natural kansui and Kiribati salt, cut at #22. The chashu is Kyoto 京の都もち豚 aged about four days, sliced thin and nearly shabu-like to showcase the pork's natural sweetness, and dessert is a house-made wasanbon pudding.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The signature bowl uses house-made wheat noodles (Kyoto "Setokirara" wheat), so the ramen contains gluten by definition. The tare/seasoning is unspecified but standard ramen tare typically contains wheat shoyu. No gluten-free menu or noodle option is advertised, and the kitchen is a single small counter operation with shared equipment. Anyone needing strict gluten avoidance should not eat the ramen here.
places.vgd: Not vegan. Although the broth is unusually animal-free for ramen — a 100% seafood dashi from two kombu varieties, Ibuki iriko (dried sardines) and saba/urume/katsuo bushi (fish flakes) with no pork or chicken stock — it is fish-based, not plant-based, and the bowl is topped with pork chashu (京の都もち豚). There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen option advertised. The kombu component is plant-derived but…

places.chef: Noriko Fujita (藤田典子) · owner, chef · Kyoto · The owner spent years as a hospital nurse, earning her nursing credentials while raising her family and returning to study around age 38 after her children grew more independent. Working grueling night shifts, she found that a bowl of ramen eaten after coming off a night shift restored both her stamina and her spirit. That comfort became a calling: at 53 she set out to open her own shop. · She refused to cut corners with wholesale noodles, investing in a professional noodle machine (from Daikoku Manufacturing, around 2.7 million yen) so she could make her own noodles in-house, because she wants customers to taste the difference of truly handmade noodles. Sitting near the universities, she also wants to send students and young people off well-fed and happy, an extension of her caretaking instincts from nursing into feeding her community. · Jiro-style ramen with generous pork and vegetable toppings; the signature is the 小豚ラーメン (kobuta / small-pork ramen). Bowls are customized at order time by noodle quantity and the classic Jiro toppings of garlic, extra vegetables, and oil.
places.gfd: No gluten-free option. This is a Jiro-style ramen shop built around house-made wheat noodles (the owner invested in a professional noodle machine specifically to make her own wheat noodles), with a typical wheat-soy-sauce tare and pork-based broth. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (Sakyo-ku, Jodoji), in the Masutani back-fat shoyu ramen tradition · Shirakawa is a small independent Kyoto-style ramen shop tucked into the Jodoji neighborhood west of Ginkaku-ji, within the Ginkakuji-michi / Kitashirakawa stretch of Sakyo-ku famous as the heartland of Kyoto back-fat shoyu ramen. The owner trained in the renowned Masutani (ますたに) lineage — the Kitashirakawa house generally credited as the origin of Kyoto's back-fat, soy-sauce-and-pork-bone style — before going out on his own to run this counter. · Faithful to old-school Kyoto ramen: an unpretentious, affordable everyday bowl served in a homey, diner-like room. A telling detail noted by writers is that vinegar is set out on the counter even though gyoza is not on the menu — a sign the owner understands that a splash of vinegar rounds out and lightens this rich Kyoto broth, a small nod to genuine Kyoto-ramen know-how. · A Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu ramen (背脂チャッチャ系): a pork-and-chicken-bone broth blanketed with melted back fat, soy-sauce tare, wheat noodles, chashu and green onion. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free noodles, or dedicated handling has been documented, and a shared broth/noodle-boiling workflow makes cross-contact likely. Not suitable for celiac diners; if avoiding gluten you should not rely on this shop.
places.vgd: The core product is a meat-based bowl: a pork/chicken-bone broth finished with back fat (背脂チャッチャ系) and topped with chashu and green onion. places.chef: chef, owner · A small independent ramen counter that opened in the summer of 2022 a short walk west of the Shijo-Omiya intersection, in the Mibu neighborhood of Kyoto's Nakagyo Ward. With just eight counter seats and a kitchen open until 2 a.m., it has built a following as a late-night spot for a carefully made bowl of chicken ramen. · The kitchen is committed to an additive-free bowl built on 100% domestic chicken, cooking the broth without chemical seasonings (muka-cho) and topping it with chicken breast and Kyoto pork. · The signature is the chicken-paitan shoyu ramen: a creamy chicken broth that the kitchen whips with an immersion blender so it turns foamy and emulsified, concentrating the savory depth, paired with fine noodles, chicken-breast chashu and green onion. The shop also pours a lighter clear chicken-dashi shoyu and shio, plus a chicken-paitan miso.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The noodles are wheat, the shoyu and miso tare are almost certainly wheat-based, and the bowls are built on a chicken broth — none of which is gluten-free. No gluten-free noodles, gluten-free tare, or celiac accommodation is advertised anywhere we could find. A celiac diner should not eat here; there is no safe bowl.
places.vgd: Every bowl is built on a 100% domestic-chicken broth (clear chicken dashi or whipped chicken paitan), and chashu toppings use chicken breast and Kyoto pork. There is no vegetable- or plant-based broth and no advertised vegan or vegetarian option. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: operator: 株式会社エフリード (F-Lead) · Yamashina, Kyoto — a casual local spot a few minutes' walk from JR / Keihan Yamashina Station. · Opened December 27, 2023 right by Yamashina Station, this compact ramen-and-onigiri counter is a produce/concept shop developed by the Nagoya-based food company F-Lead (株式会社エフリード). The idea is unusual and very deliberate: a bowl of chuka soba designed expressly to be eaten one hand on the chopsticks, the other holding a freshly formed rice ball. · Build a ramen whose flavor is tuned specifically to pair with rice — fragrant and savory rather than heavy — and serve loosely hand-formed, crumble-in-the-mouth onigiri with carefully chosen rice and generous fillings alongside it. · The headline bowl is the 生姜中華そば (ginger chuka soba): a domestic-chicken broth finished with aged re-brewed soy sauce, with ginger aroma drawn into the oil by low-temperature infusion so it reads, as one reviewer put it, 'like ginger-pork sauce with the sweetness taken out.' Thin, firm whole-grain noodles, rare-sliced chashu, red onion and menma round it out. The second pillar is the 貝だし中華そば, a clearer bowl layering scallop and clam stock.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The thin noodles are made with wheat (and contain 全粒粉/whole-grain wheat flour), the tare uses aged wheat-based soy sauce (老舗蔵元の再仕込み熟成醤油), and the onigiri are an additional wheat-free side but the ramen itself is built on wheat. Broth is chicken-and-seafood based. No dedicated gluten-free preparation or menu; a celiac diner should treat all the ramen here as unsafe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan venue. No advertised vegan or vegetarian ramen. A vegan would have essentially nothing here beyond possibly a plain rice ball, which should be confirmed…

places.chef: ramen shop, hotel café · Kyoto (Enmachi / 円町) · This is the second life of a beloved Kyoto ramen shop. The original 八の坊 (Hachinobo) opened in Enmachi on February 1, 2015 and was one of the shops that introduced Kyoto to the foam-style (泡系) ramen pioneered in Fukuoka. It later reworked itself as 八ノ家, leaning into a Yokohama-inspired family-style tonkotsu, before closing on September 30, 2023. On August 24, 2024 the name and its signature 'cappuccino' bowl were revived as Oike Café × HACHINOBO on the ground floor of Park Hotel Kyoto Oike near Karasuma-Oike. · Tame the heaviness of tonkotsu by aerating it: the frothed broth keeps the famous pork-bone aroma restrained and gives a creamy, fluffy mouthfeel, so the bowl reads as rich-but-refined rather than punishing. · Cappuccino Ramen — an ultra-rich pork-bone broth whipped into a fluffy cappuccino-like foam, served with thick curly noodles, two kinds of chashu (tender chicken and pork loin), diced onion, extra-thick menma, and a seasoned soft-boiled egg. A spicy soy-based 'RED' bowl (inspired by Katsuura tantanmen) is the other standout.
places.gfd: No gluten-free offering. The house bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare over a rich pork-bone broth — both the noodles and the tare contain wheat, so the standard bowls are not suitable for celiacs or those strictly avoiding gluten. No dedicated GF menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no allergen accommodation is documented. Anyone needing gluten-free should treat this as unsafe and confirm directly.
places.vgd: Not a vegan specialist. The signature bowls use pork-bone broth and pork/chicken chashu. places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto · The owner spent years inside Kyoto's ramen world — local accounts cite stints at established names such as Takaradoya (宝屋), Chingyu (珍遊) and Daichu (大中) — before going independent and opening this shop on June 17, 2022, taking over the former 雁木 (Gangi) ramen space on the Nakadachiuri-Chiekoin block of Kamigyo Ward. · Broad appeal over purist gatekeeping: the jiro-style bowl is positioned as a 'light jiro' with no intimidating call-out ordering system, so newcomers can try the genre without knowing the ritual. The kitchen keeps the menu wide and rotates seasonal specials (cold noodles, thin miso, extra-rich abura-soba) to stay a place anyone in the neighborhood can enjoy. · An all-rounder bowl lineup. The 中華そば (Chinese-style soba) is the everyday signature — a chicken-and-pork-bone broth (鶏ガラ豚骨ベース) with quiet depth, melt-in-the-mouth chashu and straight noodles tuned to be savory but easygoing. Alongside it the shop runs a deliberately approachable 'light jiro' (二郎系) bowl and tsukemen, plus salt, miso, seafood and niboshi variations.
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision. places.vgd: Not a vegan or vegetarian destination. The kitchen is built on animal stock — a chicken-and-pork-bone broth — across the menu, plus chashu, pork belly, and karaage sides. No plant-based bowl is offered or noted.

places.chef: family-run neighborhood shokudo · Kyoto (Meiji-era Sarashina lineage out of Shinkyogoku) · Sarashina traces its roots to a Meiji-era soba house centered on a main shop in Kyoto's Shinkyogoku shopping district; this Shogoin branch grew out of that lineage and today runs as its own quiet, independent neighborhood shokudo. You find it by walking some ten meters down a covered alley barely a meter wide — easy to stroll right past — until a low old-fashioned door opens onto a small room of rustic, folk-craft furnishings and a single mat of raised tatami seating that feels unchanged for decades. · Unfussy, neighborly cooking: an old soba shokudo that quietly serves nostalgic chuka-soba and home-style donburi at gentle prices, prizing warmth and consistency over trend. · The bowl regulars come for is the chuka-soba: pale, straight-cut Chinese noodles in a gentle, light broth that carries a subtly Japanese, dashi-leaning character rather than the heavy richness of a modern ramen-ya. It arrives piping hot and generously dressed — simmered chashu pork, menma, scallion, nori, grilled kamaboko fish cake, and pieces of wheat-gluten fu (including a pickled umefu) — the kind of comforting, every…
places.gfd: Everything central here is wheat-based: the chuka-soba noodles are Chinese wheat noodles, the soba/udon are wheat-containing, and the bowls feature wheat-gluten fu (umefu and dried fu) plus a Japanese-style broth that almost certainly relies on wheat-containing shoyu. No gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling is indicated. Not suitable for a celiac diner.
places.vgd: This is a traditional soba/udon shokudo whose dishes center on fish-and-meat dashi, pork chashu, kamaboko fish cake, and donburi over rice. The signature chuka-soba has a light broth but is topped with simmered pork chashu, menma, and grilled fish cake, and the kitchen makes no mention of plant-based options. There is no vegan offering; a vegan diner would have essentially nothing safe here.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto · The owner came up through two pillars of Kyoto's back-fat ramen tradition: he trained at the legendary Shinpuku Saikan and then served as manager (tencho) at Chinyu in Ichijoji before striking out on his own. The shop opened on November 1, 2021, in a quiet residential pocket of Minami-ku's Yoshoin district, taking over a former ramen storefront. · To serve honest, old-school Kyoto ramen (昔ながらの京都ラーメン) at neighborhood prices: the bolder, back-fat-forward seasoning that south-Kyoto locals favor, paired with the snappy medium-thin noodles that define the city's style. It is built as an approachable, family-friendly local shop rather than a destination. · The signature is a classic back-fat soy-sauce bowl (背脂醤油ラーメン) on a robustly seasoned chicken-based broth, finished with green onion, two slices of chashu, and menma. The kitchen also runs a back-fat mazesoba and a chicken bowl, plus hearty sides — beef-tendon rice bowls, karaage, and ginger-pork sets — and weekend morning ramen service.
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. This is a traditional Kyoto chuka-soba shop: wheat ramen noodles (Kondo Seimen / Kondo noodle factory), a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that almost certainly contains wheat, and chicken/pork back-fat broths. places.chef: owner-chef · Garamon began life not as a ramen shop but as a charcoal-grill yakitori izakaya called 炭焼賀ら茂ん (Sumiyaki Garamon). places.chef: second-generation owner · Yamashina, Kyoto · Yonakiya is one of the old guard of Kyoto ramen, a shop that has stood along the Nara-kaido road in the Otsuka district of Yamashina for decades and is treated as one of the originals of the city's ramen lineage. It was founded by the previous master and has since passed to the next generation, who carries on the same single-bowl tradition. · A one-bowl shop in the truest sense: it does essentially one thing, the old Kyoto chuka soba, and has done it the same way long enough that decades of consistency on a single corner are taken as proof of the cooking. · Chuka soba: relatively thin, springy straight noodles in a soy-based broth drawn from pork bone and chicken (豚骨・鶏ガラ), topped with sweet pork back-fat (背脂) that floats on the surface. The clean, delicate dashi is carried by the strength of the soy tare, so a bowl that looks rich eats surprisingly light. The shop is known for slicing its big chashu fresh to order.

places.chef: Zakoya group (seafood restaurant group) · Kyoto · Mentomeshi Zakoya is part of the Zakoya group (ZACOYA), a Kyoto seafood-focused hospitality brand running a cluster of fish-centric restaurants around Karasuma, Sanjo and Gion. The ramen concept began at a Hyakumanben main store and a Gion branch; both have since closed, and the shop relocated to its current Higashidoin-Rokkaku spot near Karasuma-Oike in February 2024. · A deliberately meat-free take on ramen: the whole bowl is built from the sea rather than pork or chicken, staying true to the Zakoya group's fish-forward identity. A playful touch is the chopstick rest - a dried sardine you can eat on its own or drop into the broth. · The signature is ryoshi-soba (fisherman's soba), a clear, light seafood ramen offered in salt (shio) and soy (shoyu) versions. The dashi is drawn from premium fish - sea bream (tai), hamo (pike conger) and kinmedai (splendid alfonsino) - built on the Zakoya group's prized fish-scrap (ara) stock, with house-made noodles and toppings of marinated, dried and seared sea bream, yuan-grilled scallop, ribbonfish (tachiuo), a seasoned egg, minced red onion and nori. The companion ryoshi-meshi rice bowl (about…
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop with house-made noodles, and the tare is almost certainly wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free noodle, or allergen accommodation was found on any page. Not suitable for celiacs. The broth is fish-based rather than pork, but the noodles and tare make the bowl unsafe for gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: Despite being meat-free (no pork or chicken), every dish is built on fish and seafood — dashi from sea bream, scallop, ribbonfish and dried sardines, with fish toppings and a seasoned egg. Not vegan or vegetarian.

places.hood: Ichijoji, Sakyo Ward (Chayama / Kyoto University of the Arts Stn)
places.notes: This is the sohonten — the original headquarters — of Tenkaippin, the cult chicken-broth ramen chain that began in Kyoto. In November 1971, founder Tsutomu Kimura, having lost his job when the gallery company he worked for went bankrupt, had a friend build him a ramen cart out of
places.chef: 木村勉 (Tsutomu Kimura) · founder · Kyoto · This is the sohonten — the original headquarters — of Tenkaippin, the cult chicken-broth ramen chain that began in Kyoto. In November 1971, founder Tsutomu Kimura, having lost his job when the gallery company he worked for went bankrupt, had a friend build him a ramen cart out of scrap metal and started pulling a yatai (food cart) around the Ginkaku-ji area. On opening night he reportedly sold only 11 bowls. He kept experimenting, and after three years and nine months he perfected the now-legendary kotteri broth. With the goodwill of a stone-mason whose lot he was using, the cart was fixed in place and grew into his first storefront in August 1975 — on this Ichijoji site, which remains the chain's spiritual home. · Kimura's idea was a broth that is 'eaten, not drunk' — a slow-cooked chicken-and-vegetable kotteri so concentrated it behaves like a sauce. The beef-tendon special was developed personally by the chairman over many trial batches, balancing the sweet-savory tendon to harmonize with that signature soup, and the recipe is kept exclusive to the sohonten. · The signature is the kotteri (こってり) bowl: a thick, almost potage-like broth si…
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The kotteri broth is built on chicken bones and vegetables, but the ramen is served with standard wheat noodles and a wheat-based shoyu tare, and the kitchen also fries gyoza, karaage and other wheat items in shared equipment. No gluten-free noodles, broth, or accommodation is offered, and there is no dedicated fryer. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. The signature broth is a long-simmered chicken-bone (鶏ガラ) and vegetable kotteri base, and the flagship-only specials are beef-tendon (牛すじ) ramen and pork rice (豚重). There are no plant-based broth, noodle, or topping options.
places.hours: 11:00-1:00 the next day (L.O. 0:45, 15 min before closing). No regular closing day (closed only on New Year's Day).

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A husband-and-wife team who began as a pop-up in the Fukakusa area, running for about three months before opening this permanent shop near Toji Station in January 2021, taking over a former Chinese-restaurant space in Minami Ward. The couple draw on their own experience raising c
places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto · A husband-and-wife team who began as a pop-up in the Fukakusa area, running for about three months before opening this permanent shop near Toji Station in January 2021, taking over a former Chinese-restaurant space in Minami Ward. The couple draw on their own experience raising children to run a warm, family-friendly counter. · The name itself is the philosophy: to thoroughly and patiently slow-simmer the chicken. The owners describe themselves as still refining the recipe, treating the bowl as a work in continual improvement. · An exceptionally concentrated chicken paitan (torigara hakutou) — the signature 'Tokoton Tori'. Chicken and a generous amount of vegetables are simmered thoroughly and gently for a long time (the literal meaning of the shop's name) into a broth so thick a ladle can stand upright in it. It is rich in collagen — enough that it sets when cooled — yet the vegetables keep the finish surprisingly clean rather than heavy. Flat noodles from Kyoto noodle maker Teikaku cling to the dense soup; sets pair the bowl with a donburi of house-made chashu, scallion, egg yolk and fried-onion shrimp oil, and fish-powder, chili and mazesoba variations are …
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The ramen uses wheat noodles (from Kyoto noodle maker Teikaku/棣鄂) and the broth is built on chicken and vegetables with a typical tare; donburi sets add chashu and other components. No gluten-free menu, dedicated prep, or allergen accommodation is mentioned by any source. Treat as unsafe for celiac diners; ask in person if highly sensitive.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian. The signature bowl is a chicken-based paitan broth (chicken simmered with vegetables); donburi sets include house-made chashu, egg yolk and shrimp oil. Although a large quantity of vegetables goes into the broth, it is fundamentally animal-based. No vegan or vegetarian option is offered.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Before opening his own shop, the owner spent roughly ten years training at one of Kyoto's most storied ramen institutions, Shinpuku Saikan (新福菜館) at Takabashi — the legendary home of jet-black soy chuka soba. He carries that Kyoto rich-soy lineage forward while adding his own ref
places.chef: owner-chef · Opened in 2020 in the Kuze district of Kyoto's Minami-ku, on the edge of Mukou City near JR Mukomachi Station. · Before opening his own shop, the owner spent roughly ten years training at one of Kyoto's most storied ramen institutions, Shinpuku Saikan (新福菜館) at Takabashi — the legendary home of jet-black soy chuka soba. He carries that Kyoto rich-soy lineage forward while adding his own refinements. · All vegetables and ingredients are domestically sourced, and the broth itself is the product of constant tinkering — described on the shop's own site as a rich-soy soup 'developed through improvement upon improvement' to land on a deep flavor with a light, clean finish. · The flagship bowl is the 醤油中華そば (rich-soy chuka soba), a concentrated pork-bone-and-soy broth that drinks surprisingly clean, finished with Kyoto's prized Kujo green onions. Other draws include the 宇宙一のまぜそば ("best-in-the-universe" maze soba), 濃厚担々麺, the vegetable-laden 京都タンメン, and a much-loved fried-rice set.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kyoto-style rich-soy chuka soba shop. The noodles are wheat, the tare is a soy-based shoyu (almost certainly containing wheat), and the broth is a concentrated pork-bone (tonkotsu) stock. No gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodles, and no published allergen accommodation. Not suitable for anyone requiring strict celiac-level avoidance of wheat.
places.vgd: Every signature bowl is built on an animal foundation: a rich pork-bone and soy broth, topped with chashu (pork). Side dishes (fried rice, gyoza, karaage, roast pork bowl) are also meat-based. The "京都タンメン" is a vegetable ramen but is served in the same animal broth, so it is not vegan. There are no published plant-based options.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Despite carrying the famous Daiichi Asahi name, this Kumano shop is not part of the celebrated honke (head shop) founded in 1947 by Kyoto Station's Takabashi. It is a survivor of an old chain expansion: when the original franchising company folded, individual shops like this one
places.chef: owner · Kyoto, Sakyo-ku (Seigoin / near Kumano Shrine) · Despite carrying the famous Daiichi Asahi name, this Kumano shop is not part of the celebrated honke (head shop) founded in 1947 by Kyoto Station's Takabashi. It is a survivor of an old chain expansion: when the original franchising company folded, individual shops like this one carried on independently, keeping the name and the recipes they had been built around. A yellowed signboard from that era — roughly four decades old — still hangs out front, a tangible piece of Kyoto ramen history. · An unpretentious, value-driven neighborhood ramen-ya: hearty, chashu-forward bowls under 1,000 yen in a retro counter setting that locals have leaned on for years. · A Kyoto-style chuka soba: a pork-bone broth that reads surprisingly light and clean despite its richness, carrying a soy tare and a faint sheen of back-fat in the classic Kyoto manner. Bowls come piled with generous chashu — diners can choose leaner thigh or richer belly cuts — over medium-thin straight noodles, with bean sprouts, scallion and a soft egg. Spicy miso can be stirred in partway through to shift the flavor.
places.gfd: This is a traditional ramen and gyoza shop. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles in a pork-bone broth with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that is almost certainly wheat-based, and gyoza wrappers are wheat — so the menu is not suitable for celiac diners. No gluten-free menu, ingredient labeling, or allergy accommodation was found in any source. A celiac diner should not eat here.
places.vgd: The shop's identity is chashu (braised pork) ramen over a pork-bone broth; gyoza are pork-filled and the bowls are topped with pork and egg. There are no vegetable or plant-based broth options noted anywhere. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: mom-and-pop neighborhood Chinese restaurant · A weathered, easy-to-miss town-Chinese shop tucked into the old streets behind Demachiyanagi, near Kyoto University. Its plain machiya-style frontage blends into the neighborhood, but the room inside is surprisingly roomy with tables and a tatami area, and it draws a steady crowd of students and locals. · Honest, filling, wallet-friendly cooking with no pretension - everything sits comfortably under 1,000 yen, and the shop keeps a calm, focused mealtime atmosphere. · Cheap, generous everyday Chinese: a simple Chinese-style ramen and fried rice, often ordered together as a set, plus big-portion plates like a heaping tenshinhan (crab-omelet rice).

The bowls rely on wheat noodles and, almost certainly, a wheat-based shoyu tare in a pork/Chinese-style broth, with shared woks and a fry station — not celiac-safe and no gluten-free preparation or menu is offered. No allergy program advertised; a celiac should not eat here.
places.vgd: A meat-and-egg town-Chinese spot: the ramen and fried rice are built on pork/animal broth, lard, egg and Chinese seasonings. No vegan or clearly plant-based dish is offered or noted, and there is no separate-pan handling, so vegans cannot reliably eat here.

places.chef: owner-operator · Kyoto (中京区, near Karasuma) · らーめん 蔵 opened on March 9, 2024 in central Kyoto near Karasuma, tucked into a Taisho-era kura (storehouse) with no street entrance of its own — diners pick up a numbered wooden tag and walk in through the BIGOLI pasta restaurant's storefront to reach the hidden eight-seat counter out back. · An almost playfully unpretentious place that leans on customer integrity: the whole shop runs on self-service — you order by lifting an antique black rotary telephone on the wall that rings straight to the kitchen, pay and make your own change, wipe down your table, and collect a 10-yen cashback yourself. The aim is honest, refined Kyoto flavor at a remarkably low price for the city center. · 京出汁醤油らーめん in three 'bloom' grades — つぼみ (bud, no chashu), 五分咲き (half-bloom, some chashu) and 満開 (full bloom, generous chashu) — built on a gentle Kyoto-style dashi of kombu and fish stock with white dashi, finished with a honjozo soy-sauce tare and a touch of fragrant mayu burnt oil. Hand-kneaded crimped wheat noodles come from the well-known Kyoto maker 麺屋棣鄂, and bowls are topped with thin pork-belly chashu, green onion and Kansai-style crispy aburakasu (fried…
places.gfd: This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop with no gluten-free offering. The signature 京出汁醤油らーめん uses crimped hand-kneaded wheat noodles from Kyoto noodle maker 麺屋棣鄂, and the soy-sauce tare is made from honjozo/hon-mirin soy sauce (wheat-containing). Broth, noodles, and tare all contain wheat, and the cold つけ麺 is likewise wheat-based. Not safe for celiac diners.

places.n: スタメン (Stamen (Start With Men))
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Stamen (stylized START WITH MEN) opened in January 2023 in the Kashihara residential district of Nishikyo Ward, a roughly 20-minute walk from Hankyu Katsura/Rakusaiguchi. It is the second brand and third shop of the well-loved Kyoto ramen maker Ramen Mugyu, whose flagship sits in
places.chef: ramen shop, sister brand of Ramen Mugyu · Kyoto (Nishikyo Ward) · Stamen (stylized START WITH MEN) opened in January 2023 in the Kashihara residential district of Nishikyo Ward, a roughly 20-minute walk from Hankyu Katsura/Rakusaiguchi. It is the second brand and third shop of the well-loved Kyoto ramen maker Ramen Mugyu, whose flagship sits in the Enmachi (Marutamachi) area. · Described as a brushed-up, new-generation take on classic Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu ramen — refined and approachable rather than extreme, aimed at pleasing both young diners and families. The parent brand sums up its priorities as 自慢のスープ、こだわりの焼き豚 (a soup it is proud of and meticulously made roast pork), and the kitchen wraps up service once the day's chashu runs out. · The signature is a back-fat shoyu ramen: a clear pork stock (豚清湯) generously crowned with chunks of melted back fat, balanced by negi, bean sprouts and chashu, served with medium-thick slightly-wavy wheat noodles from the established maker Teigaku. A wonton-men (ワンタンメン) and a richer 濃厚 bowl round out the lineup, with gyoza, fried rice and karaage as sides.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls use medium-thick wheat ramen noodles (from producer Teigaku) and a shoyu (soy sauce) tare over a pork broth, plus gyoza, fried rice and karaage on the menu. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and there is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, tare, or dedicated handling. Not suitable for celiac diners; treat as not GF-safe.
places.vgd: A pork-broth (豚清湯) ramen specialist whose signature is back-fat shoyu ramen with chashu pork; the brand explicitly centers on its soup and its hand-prepared roast pork (焼き豚), and sides are gyoza, fried rice and karaage. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered. Vegans cannot eat here.
places.hours: Tue-Fri 11:00-15:30 / 17:00-21:30, Sat and Sun 11:00-21:30 (continuous), closed Mon. Official site lists 11:00-21:30 (L.O. 21:00). Closes once chashu sells out.

places.n: 辛獅子 本店 (Karajishi Honten)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small specialist ramen counter in Kyoto's Nishioji-Sanjo / Gozen-Sanjo area, devoted entirely to karaimen — Korean-influenced spicy noodles built around a fiery minced-meat, garlic, scallion and egg broth.
places.chef: owner · A small specialist ramen counter in Kyoto's Nishioji-Sanjo / Gozen-Sanjo area, devoted entirely to karaimen — Korean-influenced spicy noodles built around a fiery minced-meat, garlic, scallion and egg broth. · '辛いが旨い' — spicy, but delicious: the heat is meant to amplify flavor, not bury it. · The house spicy bowl, where diners dial in heat from 0辛 (no spice) up through extreme levels (each step past the base adds a small charge), choosing either curly egg noodles or the shop's signature thin or thick 'konnyaku' noodles. The braised pork-cartilage rice bowl (なんこつ丼) — pork rib cartilage simmered until meltingly tender and finished with a ginger-grilled-style sauce — is a celebrated second act.
places.gfd: No gluten-free offering. The spicy bowl uses either curly egg noodles (wheat) or "konnyaku" noodles that are in fact made primarily from buckwheat/wheat flour rather than pure konjac, plus a spicy minced-meat tare and toppings such as garlic and scallion. There is no indication of a wheat-free broth, tare, or dedicated preparation, so this is not safe for celiac diners. Treat as not gluten-free; anyone highly sensitive should avoid.
places.vgd: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The kitchen is built around spicy noodles topped with minced meat and egg, and the celebrated sides are braised pork cartilage (nankotsu) and a pork-cartilage rice bowl. Eggs feature throughout (egg noodles, raw/soft egg toppings). No plant-based ramen is advertised. A "0辛" (no-spice) version exists but only changes heat, not the animal content.
places.hours: 09:00-15:30 (L.O. 14:50, closes once soup runs out). Irregular days off (often Fri).

places.n: 魔界系ラーメン三冠馬 (Makaikei Ramen Sankanba)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, family-run ramen shop that opened in September 2022 in the Saiin/Nishikyogoku area of Kyoto's Ukyo ward. The interior is filled with horse-racing memorabilia, plush toys, and posters reflecting the owner's deep love of the sport.
places.chef: owner, chef · The owner trained with and was supported by the popular Sendai shop 'Makai Ramen Gekko' (魔界ラーメン 月光) when opening, which is the source of the 'makai-kei' (魔界系) name describing the intense, rich broth lineage. · A small, family-run ramen shop that opened in September 2022 in the Saiin/Nishikyogoku area of Kyoto's Ukyo ward, in a former Chinese-restaurant space. The interior is filled with horse-racing memorabilia, plush toys, and posters reflecting the owner's deep love of the sport. · An at-home, easygoing neighborhood spot where the owner's passion for both ramen and horse racing sets the tone. · Three signature bowls: '衝撃の豚' (a thick, creamy pork-bone and fish shoyu ramen), '黄金の鶏' (a golden chicken ramen), and '皇帝の油そば' (an emperor's aburasoba/brothless mixed noodle). The pork-bone fish bowl is praised as concentrated and mellow yet clean, with backbone-deep umami and none of the heaviness you might expect.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles with a soy-based (wheat shoyu) tare and a thick pork-bone and fish broth, so they are not safe for celiacs. No GF menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling is advertised.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. All three signature bowls are animal-based: pork-bone/fish broth and chicken broth, with pork chashu and egg toppings. No plant-based or vegetable broth option is offered.
