places.n: 笑福屋 (Shofukuya)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Shofukuya is a small neighborhood ramen shop near Hankyu Nishikyogoku station, run by an owner who trained as a sushi/Japanese-cuisine chef (元板前) before opening here. That washoku pedigree is what sets the place apart: locals and writers consistently point to the kitchen's precis
places.chef: owner-chef · Shofukuya is a small neighborhood ramen shop near Hankyu Nishikyogoku station, run by an owner who trained as a sushi/Japanese-cuisine chef (元板前) before opening here. That washoku pedigree is what sets the place apart: locals and writers consistently point to the kitchen's precision with fish and rice as the reason a ramen shop turns out sushi-restaurant-quality side dishes. · A ramen shop seen through a sushi chef's eyes — restrained, balanced broth rather than heavy intensity, and the same care with fish and rice you'd expect at a sushi counter. · The signature bowl is a soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen built on a pork-bone and chicken-carcass base finished with a fish/dried-sardine dashi — light and approachable on the first sip but deepening into a quiet umami richness. A delicate shio (salt) ramen is offered in the evenings. But the dish the shop is most loved for is the zuke-don: vinegared sushi rice topped with nori, fresh wasabi, and thick-cut marinated yellowtail (hamachi), often available as a 1,000-yen ramen-and-zuke-don set and sold in limited quantity until it runs out.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation. This is a standard wheat-noodle ramen shop whose broth is a pork-bone/chicken-carcass base finished with a fish-infused soy-sauce (shoyu) tare — the tare is wheat-based shoyu and the noodles are wheat. No celiac-safe options were found in any source, and the kitchen makes no allergen claims. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The ramen broths are animal-based (pork bone + chicken carcass, plus dried-fish/niboshi dashi), and the signature side dishes are seafood (marinated yellowtail zuke-don, sashimi). No plant-based or vegetarian ramen was found in any source.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Takaraya was once a fast-growing name in Kyoto's ramen world, with a flagship in Pontocho and branches in Fushimi-Momoyama, Mibu, the Kyoto Ramen Koji food hall and beyond. When the operating company went bankrupt in 2011, most of those shops closed or changed hands, and the surv
places.chef: independent ramen shop · Kyoto · Takaraya was once a fast-growing name in Kyoto's ramen world, with a flagship in Pontocho and branches in Fushimi-Momoyama, Mibu, the Kyoto Ramen Koji food hall and beyond. When the operating company went bankrupt in 2011, most of those shops closed or changed hands, and the survivors reopened under new names such as Kourai (香来), Shinrai (神来) and Miyako (京). The Nishikoji-Gojo branch is the one and only shop still trading under the original 宝屋 name. · Keep serving the unchanged, honest taste of an old-Kyoto ramen at an everyday price — bowls have long started around 600 to 800 yen — so the neighborhood always has its classic back-fat bowl to come home to. · The signature is a Kyoto-classic back-fat pork-bone shoyu bowl: a glossy 背脂 (back-fat) shoyu broth on a pork- and chicken-bone base, paired with the shop's namesake 熟成細麺 — aged thin noodles that stay firm with a springy, shikoshiko bite. Beloved companion orders include the char-siu ramen (チャーシューメン), the fatty toro-niku char-siu bowl, and the layered char-siu rice bowl (チャー丼).
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. The shop's identity is built on wheat "熟成細麺" (aged thin wheat noodles) served in a back-fat pork-bone shoyu broth, and the tare is a wheat-based soy sauce. Noodles, broth tare, and gyoza all contain wheat; cross-contamination from a shared noodle-boiling pot and wok is unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-sensitive diners.

places.chef: owner · Tokyo / Higashi-Ikebukuro Taishoken lineage, adapted for Kyoto · This is a Kyoto branch of the legendary 東池袋大勝軒, the Tokyo shop in the Higashi-Ikebukuro district credited as the birthplace of tsukemen. The dish was born by accident in the 1950s: while working at the original shop, owner Kazuo Yamagishi would eat noodles dipped in broth, zaru-soba style, as a quick staff meal; a regular customer saw it and asked to try the same, and from 1955 it joined the menu as tsukemen. · A defining Kyoto touch: because tsukemen began as a staff meal meant to be eaten fast, the dipping broth was traditionally served only lukewarm, but here it is served piping hot for local tastes. The dip is lighter and a touch sweeter than today's intensely thick tsukemen, loaded with chashu, menma and narutomaki, with seafood aromatics that bloom when you add soup to the leftover broth at the end. · Tsukemen (dipping noodles) — chewy, thick-cut wheat noodles served alongside a sweet-leaning dipping broth that blends chicken bones, pork bones and seafood. The signature pair is the 元祖つけ麺 (original) and the 濃厚つけ麺 (rich, finished with fish powder); an atsumori option serves the noodles piping hot.
places.gfd: Tsukemen and ramen built on thick wheat noodles, with a chicken-pork-seafood dipping broth that is almost certainly seasoned with wheat-based shoyu tare. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, broth, or any allergy accommodation. This shop is not safe for celiacs; cross-contamination from a shared wheat-noodle kitchen is unavoidable.
places.vgd: A classic meat-and-fish tsukemen house: the broth combines chicken bones, pork bones and seafood, and bowls come topped with chashu (pork), menma and narutomaki. There are no vegan or vegetarian options noted.

places.chef: Osamu Shinkai · owner, chef · Tokyo · Osamu Shinkai, a Tokyo native, spent years as a head chef in hotel Chinese and yakiniku kitchens before relocating to Kyoto in 2023 to open his own counter shop devoted to a single idea. · Rather than building a bowl around a rich broth, the shop strips the soup away entirely so the noodles themselves take center stage, with a sauce blended in a 'golden ratio' meant to flatter the noodle and let diners boldly mix and customize to taste. · Taresoba (soupless mixed noodles): the signature soy-sauce bowl tops springy noodles with pork-belly chashu, chopped onion, white sesame, scallion and bamboo shoot, which you mix vigorously with a tare of special soy sauce, oil, white vinegar and umami chili oil before eating; spicy and chilled mustard-sauce versions round out the lineup.

places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian options. Every taresoba bowl comes with pork-belly chashu, and toppings/sides lean on meat (assorted chashu, mini chashu rice bowl) and egg (onsen tamago). The tare is soy-sauce based with no advertised plant-only build. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl.
places.chef: Sakakimoto · owner, chef · This is the second outpost of the Jun chicken-paitan brand, following the original near Marutamachi; it opened in the Shijo-Karasuma area on August 13, 2025. · Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl. · Sakakimoto has said that if he was going to open his own place, he wanted to do something only he could do — hence the labor-intensive, single-serving emulsified broth and the kappo-trained attention to finish and presentation. · The signature is a tori-paitan (chicken white-soup) soba in an espuma-like, foamed broth. Rather than ladling from one big pot, the kitchen emulsifies the chicken soup bowl by bowl in a blender, whipping it into a mild, airy, almost cappuccino-like froth. The base is built primarily on Kagoshima chicken, rounded out with small amounts of Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and paired with custom medium-thick, chewy noodles and rare pork chashu.
places.gfd: This is a chicken-paitan ramen specialist built around custom medium-thick wheat noodles served in a creamy chicken-and-pork-bone broth, with seasoning tare and shoyu/miso variants that typically contain wheat. places.vgd: Every bowl is built on an animal base: a rich chicken (tori-paitan) broth made primarily with Kagoshima chicken, supplemented with Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and topped with rare pork chashu. places.chef: ramen shop, izakaya offshoot · Kyoto · Toyojiro opened on December 1, 2024 in the Kawaramachi/Kiyamachi area of Kyoto (Yaoyacho, Nakagyo-ku), growing out of the popular tuna-and-wagyu izakaya Toyota (とよ田) and sharing its premises. It represents that team's leap from sake-side beef and tuna plates into a dedicated Jiro-style ramen concept. · To elevate the famously rough, fat-heavy Jiro genre with high-grade wagyu fat rather than ordinary pork back-fat, aiming for a smooth, deep umami that gives ramen fans a more refined take on the style. · A wagyu-forward Jiro-style bowl: a broth built on rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle from Okazaki Ranch, finished with a soy-sauce or salt tare and crowned with premium wagyu fat. places.vgd: A Jiro-style ramen shop built around a beef-fat broth (rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle), wheat noodles, and beef-tendon (bokkake) toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian bowl here; the entire concept is meat-forward, so a plant-based diner has nothing safe to order.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto · Menya Ichiki bills itself as a Kyoto white-miso ramen specialist. It first opened on October 6, 2025 as a tucked-away shop in the Nishijin area, then relocated and reopened on April 22, 2026 in a renovated Kyoto townhouse (machiya) in Shikino Higashino-cho, Kita Ward, along Kitaoji-dori near Kenkun Shrine and Daitoku-ji. · The shop leans into local Kyoto identity — white miso, yuba and fu — to set its bowls apart from typical tonkotsu or shoyu ramen, and keeps a calm, welcoming room where even solo diners are at ease. · The signature bowl is the 京の白味噌らーめん (Kyo no Shiro-miso Ramen): an original tare blending several Kyoto white misos for a gently sweet, creamy soup, married to a bonito-and-kombu dashi. A variation, the 京の白味噌貝だしらーめん, swaps in a shellfish (scallop) dashi for a mellower umami. Bowls come dressed in distinctly Kyoto ingredients — fresh yuba (tofu skin) and fresh fu (wheat gluten) — alongside smoked chashu pork, a soft-boiled egg, white negi and bonito flakes. The chashu is torched just before serving to coax out its aroma and umami. Thick, straight noodles with a firm chew round it out. A rice-and-fried-chicken set can be added.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles and is topped with fresh fu (生麩, wheat gluten), so there are multiple unavoidable wheat sources in the dish itself. The broth is a white-miso tare with bonito/kombu dashi (miso typically contains wheat or barley as well). No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or celiac accommodation is indicated. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here safely.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian. Both signature bowls are built on animal stock — bonito (katsuobushi)/kombu dashi or a shellfish (kai) dashi — and are topped with smoked chashu pork and a soft-boiled egg. While the yuba (tofu skin) and fresh fu toppings are plant-based, the broth foundation is fish/shellfish-based, so the ramen is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. No vegan version is advertised.
places.hours: 11:00-15:00 / 17:00-20:30 (may close once soup runs out). Closed days irregular - specific weekday closures not published, so the same hours are listed for all days with an irregular-schedule flag.

places.chef: owner-operator · Kumamoto-style ramen · A small ramen counter sitting steps from Kitayama Station and across from the Kyoto Prefectural Botanical Garden, serving the Kumamoto style of tonkotsu in a city better known for lighter Kyoto ramen. The name itself is a wink to its roots: 'mokkosu' is Kumamoto dialect for a stubborn, headstrong, true-to-yourself sort of person. · Diners describe an owner with a meticulous, conscientious touch in the service and presentation, leaning into a robust, full-bodied bowl rather than the lighter Hakata-style tonkotsu. · Kumamoto ramen: a thick, milky-white tonkotsu (pork-bone) broth finished with fragrant burnt-garlic ma-yu oil, served with thin, straight noodles. A favorite side is the paiku rice (パイクごはん): pork rib cartilage braised sweet-and-spicy until meltingly tender, collagen-rich and juicy, served over rice.

places.vgd: The entire menu is built on a rich pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth with pork toppings, plus chicken karaage and soy-braised pork rice. No vegetarian or vegan ramen is offered.

places.chef: owner · Saiin, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto · Iwamotoya occupies the former 麺匠 一粒万倍 西院店, a branch of a Kyoto ramen group known for lighter chicken-based (Oyama jidori and duck) clear shoyu bowls. That Saiin location — the one shop in the group that had long served iekei — closed on August 3, 2025 and reopened on August 11, 2025 as a dedicated Yokohama-style iekei (家系) tonkotsu-shoyu shop aimed at late-night and younger diners in the Saiin area. · Rather than leaning on surface oil, the shop builds its identity on a genuinely concentrated, dense broth that still keeps a proper drinkable fluidity — an honest take on iekei conventions that aims for real depth of bone-and-marrow character rather than formulaic repetition. · The signature bowl is a straightforward iekei 'Ramen' (around 950 yen): a thick pork-and-chicken bone broth with a soy tare, topped in classic family-style fashion with a slice of chashu pork, spinach, and three sheets of nori. The noodles are sourced from Tokyo's well-known Sugano Seimen (菅野製麺所) and served a touch shorter than typical iekei noodles, with a rice pairing available.
places.gfd: This is a Yokohama iekei (家系) ramen shop built on wheat ramen noodles (from Tokyo's Sugano Seimen / 菅野製麺所), a wheat-based shoyu tare, and a thick pork-and-chicken bone broth — none of which is gluten-free. No gluten-free noodles, tare, or menu options are advertised, and there is no indication of allergen handling. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
places.vgd: A pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken broth iekei specialist; the signature bowl is topped with chashu pork, spinach, and nori. The broth, tare, and toppings are animal-based with no vegan or vegetarian ramen offered. Not suitable for vegans.

places.chef: UNCHI株式会社 (operator) · Osaka, Japan (chain origin) · This is the first Kyoto location of くそオヤジ最後のひとふり, a clam-broth ramen brand under Osaka's UNCHI Co., the company behind the celebrated 'Jinrui Mina Menrui' (人類みな麺類). places.vgd: This is a shellfish-broth ramen specialist — every bowl (asari/shijimi/hamaguri) is built on a clam dashi with soy-sauce tare and contains clams; there are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options.

places.chef: owner-chef · 麺心よし田 is the shop Fushimi locals name first when the talk turns to tsukemen. Tucked just west of Fushimi-Momoyama / Momoyama-Goryomae stations, past the Otesuji shopping arcade, it has built a devoted following over years — regulars describe coming back dozens of times since their student days for noodles that taste reliably the same. · The heart of the shop is the house-made noodle — milled from Nagano stone-ground whole-grain flour blended with refined wheat, giving a soba-like fragrance. The classic alternative is a chicken-and-seafood (鶏魚介) dip.

The dipping broths are wheat-thickened/seasoned and rich in shrimp, chicken and fish. There is no gluten-free noodle or menu, no dedicated equipment, and noodles are boiled in shared water — not suitable for celiac diners.

places.chef: Miyaji Tamotsu · Cantonese kitchen, tantanmen specialist, family-run · Muko City (Teradocho), Kyoto · Kirin-en opened in 1967, when authentic Cantonese cooking was still a rarity in the then-farmland district of Muko. Founder Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) set out to let local residents enjoy genuine Guangdong cuisine casually, and the place has stayed family-run, with Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮) now serving as store manager. · The house motto for its spicy dishes is 「辛くて旨い」— 'spicy but delicious' (うま辛) — chasing flavor and craft rather than heat for its own sake. · A fiery tantanmen built on four kinds of chili plus a house-made meat-miso for depth, which became the restaurant's calling card during Muko City's spicy-food (gekikara) town-revitalization push. In developing it the kitchen reached for the bhut jolokia ('jolokia') pepper — once billed as the world's hottest — and the bowl can be ordered across escalating heat levels (roughly 1 to 5), with the mild steps served without the jolokia powder and the hottest tiers dosed with it.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation found. This is a Cantonese Chinese restaurant whose signature is a chili-laden tantanmen — wheat noodles in a sesame/chili broth, almost certainly built on a wheat-based shoyu/miso tare and a pork base. No allergen or gluten-free information is published on the official site, and nothing indicates celiac-safe handling. A celiac diner should treat this place as not safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan venue. A traditional Cantonese kitchen with a meat- and seafood-forward menu (the famous tantanmen and black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork are both meat dishes). No vegan ramen or vegan set is advertised, and tantanmen broth is typically pork/sesame based. A vegan would need to ask, with little likelihood of a fully plant-based bowl.

places.chef: independent local ramen shop · Kyoto (Nishijin / Uzumasa) · A modest, locally beloved ramen shop in the Nishijin district of Kyoto's Kamigyo ward, set along Chiekoin-dori (知恵光院通) near the old textile quarter. It is the second location (2号店) of Ramen Tengu, whose main shop is in Uzumasa in western Kyoto, and it carries a nostalgic Showa-era chuka-soba feel with a hand-painted sign and a cozy room of wrap-around counter and a few low tatami seats. · Keep it simple and let the broth do the work - a clean, comforting Kyoto-style bowl that regulars return for rather than a flashy specialty shop. · The house bowl, Tengu Ramen, is built on a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese-style dashi: it looks rich and is dressed with back-fat, yet drinks surprisingly clean and stays balanced to the last sip. It comes over thin, springy noodles with menma, nori and a chashu so slow-braised it falls apart and melts on the tongue. A generous heap of fresh, crisp scallions is served on the side so you can pile them in to taste, with an extra-scallion (追いネギ) option for about 50 yen.
places.gfd: A wheat-noodle ramen shop. The signature bowl is thin wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese dashi, almost certainly built on a wheat-based shoyu tare, with chashu and menma. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, a dedicated preparation area, or allergen handling, and broth/tare are shared. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: The base of every bowl is an animal broth (pork bone blended with Japanese dashi), and toppings center on braised pork chashu. No vegetable or vegan broth, no plant-based ramen, and no meatless menu is described. Not a vegan-friendly option.

places.chef: owner-chef (former Sugichiyo head cook) · Tokiwa (near Uzumasa), Ukyo-ku, Kyoto · Opened in 2002 by a chef who had headed the kitchen (店長／元料理長) at Sugichiyo (杉千代), a legendary Uzumasa ramen shop that drew lines for its then-revolutionary bowls some two decades ago. When Sugichiyo's original shop was gone, Tengu became the refuge for its devoted fans — described as the sole shop carrying Sugichiyo's DNA forward — and it is the original 2002 shop of the Ramen Kyoto Tengu group. · Carry the Sugichiyo lineage faithfully rather than chase trends: an honest, additive-conscious pork-bone shoyu bowl in a modest storefront, kept welcoming for families, children and women rather than dressed up as a destination shop. · Tengu Ramen (てんぐラーメン): a pork-bone and chicken-gara shoyu broth finished with back fat (背脂) that drinks lighter than it looks, paired with thin low-alkaline straight noodles in the Sugichiyo mold and chashu so tender it falls apart when lifted with chopsticks. A basket of chopped green onion is provided to season the bowl to taste, and rice is famously all-you-can-eat.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop: the noodles are thin low-alkaline wheat noodles (mirroring the Sugichiyo lineage), the tare is soy-sauce based (shoyu, which in Japan virtually always contains wheat), and gyoza/shumai/shoronpo sides are wheat-wrapped. The pork-bone/chicken broth itself plus heavy shared-pot/shared-fryer use means cross-contamination is unavoidable. No gluten-free menu or noodle substitute is offered.
places.vgd: Not a vegan or vegetarian establishment. The signature bowl is built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken-gara broth finished with back fat (背脂), topped with chashu pork. The broth and the standard bowls are animal-based, so there are no genuine vegan or vegetarian ramen options here. A plant-based diner would have no suitable main; ask staff before ordering, but expect no accommodation.
places.hours: Lunch and dinner 11:30-2:00 the next day (L.O. 1:40). No regular closing day.

places.chef: owner, ramen chef · Kyoto (Umezu, Ukyo-ku) · A small ramen specialist tucked into the Umezu neighborhood of Kyoto's Ukyo ward, on the Arashiyama side of the city near the Hankyu Matsuo-taisha line. The shop has been quietly perfecting one thing for over four decades, opening around 1981 and, in the owner's own words, building it up steadily over roughly 45 years in a corner of Kyoto. · The owner's stated aim is simple and warm: once a customer comes in, to earn their return and become a shop they patronize for a lifetime - 'a lifelong asset.' Guests are invited to step in without hesitation and give the ramen a try. · The signature bowl is a Kyoto-style shoyu ramen in the Daiichi-Asahi (第一旭) mold: a pork clear-broth (tonkotsu seitan) made from Miyazaki-raised pork, seasoned with a light soy-sauce tare. Unlike many Kyoto bowls it skips the heavy back-fat float yet still drinks rich, with a generous layer of oil on top - mild in flavor but satisfyingly hearty. It comes crowned with soft, fatty melt-in-the-mouth chashu, thin bean sprouts, and Kujo green onion over thin, low-hydration straight noodles.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kyoto-style ramen shop. The bowl is built on wheat noodles in a pork-based clear broth seasoned with a light soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is wheat-based. Both the noodles and the tare contain wheat/gluten, and there is no gluten-free menu, no separate preparation, and no indication of allergy accommodation. This is not safe for celiacs or those avoiding gluten.
places.vgd: Every bowl is built on a pork bone broth (made from Miyazaki-raised pork) and topped with fatty chashu pork, so the soup itself is animal-based. There are no vegan or vegetarian options on the menu.

places.chef: owner-operated, Chinese-staffed kitchen · Higashiyama, Kyoto · Ryumon is widely regarded as one of Kyoto's pioneers of authentic Sichuan cooking, with its original Higashiyama-Sanjo location anchoring a small family of about four branches across the city. places.chef: 深谷信人 (Fukaya) · owner-chef · Kyoto (Nishikyo-ku, Kashihara) · Rosen is a small, calm house restaurant in the Kashihara neighborhood of Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, a short walk from Hankyu Katsura Station. Owner-chef Fukaya (深谷信人), a Kameoka native, trained from his teens — culinary school, then the celebrated Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) that once sat in Kyoto's Holiday Inn, followed by kitchens in Osaka and Nishinomiya — before going solo to Shanghai to study authentic Chinese cooking. He named the shop after Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan and opened in Kashihara about a dozen years ago, and he still hand-makes his doubanjiang, tianmianjiang and douchi and cooks with Kashihara- and Kameoka-grown vegetables. · Authentic Sichuan and Chinese cooking served generously and affordably in an unfussy, settled space — confident portions and honest pricing rather than show, built on house-made seasonings and local produce. · Tantan-men is the house signature, offered in white-sesame and black-sesame versions (with a curry tantan-men alongside). The black-sesame bowl is the standout: a rich, deeply aromatic sesame sauce with gentle sweetness and restrained heat over springy noodles — mellow rat…
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision found. The house specialty is tantan-men, which is wheat noodles in a sesame-rich, meat-based sauce, and the kitchen is a Sichuan/Chinese operation that relies on wheat-based soy sauce and fermented bean paste (doubanjiang). Mapo tofu, yakisoba, and other listed dishes are all gluten-bearing. No dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen labeling, and no cross-contamination controls were documented anywhere. Treat as not celiac-safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan or vegetarian-oriented shop. places.chef: Shoichi Iwasaki · owner, head chef · Opened March 2013 in the Nishinokyō neighborhood of Kyoto's Nakagyō Ward, near Nijō Castle and the Sanjō-kai shopping arcade. · Owner-chef Shoichi Iwasaki (岩﨑昭一) spent roughly 15 years training at a celebrated tonkotsu ramen shop in Minoh, Osaka — also his hometown — before opening Yoshiharu on March 11, 2013. After leaving the kitchen where he learned his craft, he spent extensive trial-and-error developing the broth that would become the shop's signature. · Iwasaki aims for a broth that suppresses the heavy off-odor often associated with pork bone, delivering deep umami and richness with a clean, light finish — a balance of 'umami, richness, and depth.' places.chef: female owner · Kyoto — a new concept from the three-generation Motomachi Ramen family, set in a renovated traditional wooden machiya on Ninenzaka. · ichiren is a newer yuzu-ramen specialist tucked into an alley just off Ninenzaka, a couple of minutes' walk below Kiyomizu-dera and Kodai-ji, opened May 16, 2021. It is a fresh brand launched by the family behind Motomachi Ramen (元町ラーメン), a Kyoto ramen name carried across three generations, so the bowls draw on a long local lineage while being reworked into something refined and contemporary. · To carry forward Kyoto tradition while evolving it into a refined, distinctly Kyoto ramen — built around yuzu and a calm white-and-yuzu-toned interior meant to be welcoming for solo diners and especially women. · Yuzu-forward Kyoto ramen. The namesake 一蓮 (Ichiren) is a rich double broth of pork bone and chicken bones brightened with yuzu; 紗 (Sara) is a clearer fish-dashi bowl (grilled flying fish, bonito, mackerel, sardine) also scented with yuzu; and the 豆乳柚子 (soy milk yuzu) bowl is creamy yet light. Bowls come with tsukune, and tables offer tororo kombu, yuzu-shichimi and yuzu-kosho to shift the flavor mid-meal.
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision. This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop: the signature bowls use thin/thick wheat noodles in pork-and-chicken or fish-dashi broths, and standard ramen tare contains wheat-based soy sauce. places.chef: independent ramen shop / chan-noren guild member · Ono, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto · Akichan Ramen opened on September 4, 2025, a short walk from Ono Station near Zuishin-in temple, becoming what local press called the first 'chan-kei' (ちゃん系) ramen shop to land in Kyoto. It belongs to the Chan-noren guild (ちゃんのれん組合), a federation of Tokyo shops such as Kanda Chie-chan, Shinjuku Ecchan, and Ikebukuro Hiro-chan that brought this style westward. · Faithfully recreate the Kanto 'chan-kei' bowl — layered umami, rendered pork fat richness, and a clean clear broth — for Kyoto diners, with noodles kept slightly separate from the broth for texture. · Chuka soba (中華そば) — a Tokyo-style clear, fat-rich pork broth with sharp soy-and-salt seasoning, served with generous chashu pork belly, deeply flavored bamboo shoots, and white negi over flat, smooth specialty noodles from Shinjuku Daruma Seimensho. A favorite move is adding a raw egg to mellow the saltiness, often paired with negi rice.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free / not celiac-safe. The dish is wheat ramen noodles (flat noodles from Shinjuku Daruma Seimensho) in a soy-seasoned broth (wheat-based shoyu tare typical of the style). No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodations are mentioned anywhere.
places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian options. The signature chuka soba is built on a pork-based clear broth (清湯) with sharp soy/salt seasoning and is topped with chashu pork belly, so the broth and standard bowls contain animal products.

places.chef: owner-chef · Fushimi-ku, Kyoto — a ramen battleground near Ryukoku University · The owner is a well-known local Jiro-style ramen proprietor long tied to this Fushimi corner on Shidan-dori. Over the years he has run several shops in the area — 'Ramen Dai,' 'Gatts K Ramen,' and 'Ryu no Sakura' — and completed a short training stint at 'Yume o Katare,' the celebrated Jiro-style shop. After stepping away, he returned to the neighborhood, on the spot that once housed 'Ramen Dai,' to open this shop in summer 2024. · The shop name '夢は力なり' means 'a dream is strength' — an aspirational banner from an owner who left and came back to feed his old neighborhood, carrying the lineage of the Jiro-style shops he trained in and ran before. · A non-emulsified Jiro bowl: a clean, sharply soy-forward, non-emulsified shoyu broth (rather than the thick cloudy emulsified style), paired with house-made wavy ultra-thick chewy noodles, big chunks of pork, a boiled egg, and a hit of black pepper. Diners customize with the free 'call' system — extra vegetables, oil (abura), and garlic — over generous portions (roughly 300g standard). Aburasoba-style eating is part of the appeal.

This is a Jiro-style ramen shop built around house-made ultra-thick wheat noodles and a soy (shoyu) tare, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat. The broth is pork-based and bowls are loaded with wheat noodles, so gluten is unavoidable. No gluten-free menu, noodle substitute, or allergen accommodation is advertised. Abura soba (brothless) is also wheat noodles. Treat as off-limits if you require strict GF.

places.chef: owner-operator · Demachiyanagi, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · 鴨町らーめん is a tiny counter-only ramen shop (about nine seats) tucked into the Demachi neighborhood a minute's walk east of Demachiyanagi Station, on a stretch with surprisingly few eateries that makes it a reliable local stop. places.chef: owner-operator · Kyoto · Opened February 7, 2026 in the Nishi-Kamogamo / Omiya-Yakushiyama corner of Kita-ku, taking over a space that had previously housed another ramen shop. It is a small independent counter built around one idea: a Kyoto bowl you could eat every single day. · "毎日食べられるラーメン" — ramen you can eat every day. The seasoning is kept gentle on purpose, the chashu is cooked soft so it appeals across all ages, and the noodles are made in-house: medium-thick angular straight noodles at 25% hydration, rested a day, with egg white worked in to push the wheat aroma that Kyoto diners favor. · The house pork-shoyu ramen. The broth is a pork clear-soup (豚清湯) made from only pork arm meat and back fat — deliberately no pork bone — so it lands light yet rich ("あっさりコクうま"), then seasoned with Goko (五光), a traditional Kyoto soy sauce, for that familiar nostalgic Kyoto sharpness. The signature move is chashu, piled without restraint: the standard Buta-yado Ramen (¥950) carries 150g, and the Buta-yado Chashu-men (¥1,200) goes to a 210g mountain of tender, thinly-sliced pork arm. A lighter Buta-yasumi Ramen (¥700) keeps just 30g for a quieter bowl.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The bowls are built on house-made wheat noodles (中太の角ストレート麺 with egg white added for a wheat aroma), seasoned with Kyoto Goko soy sauce tare, which is wheat-based. No gluten-free noodle or tare option is offered and no allergy/cross-contamination handling is described anywhere. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner cannot safely eat the ramen here.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The entire concept is pork-centric: the broth is made solely from animal ingredients (豚ウデ肉・背脂 — pork arm meat and back fat), and the shop's identity is generous chashu (sliced pork). The soy-sauce tare and side dishes are pork-based as well. There is no vegetable broth or plant-based bowl.

places.chef: owner · 麺屋 月 is a small abura-soba specialist that opened on February 22, 2026 in Kyoto's Shimogamo neighborhood, on Kitaoji-dori near Kyoto Prefectural University in what is a competitive local ramen district. places.chef: Saifullah · owner · Kyoto · Ayam-YA grew out of a ramen company whose very first shop opened not in Japan but in Seattle. When the team brought the concept home to Japan's hyper-competitive ramen scene, they struggled to draw crowds, until an Indonesian exchange student asked a simple question that changed everything: 'Do you use only chicken?' That was the moment the founders learned that many visitors could not eat ordinary ramen for religious reasons. Determined to let Muslim travelers in Kyoto enjoy a real bowl of Japanese ramen with peace of mind, they reformulated the recipe and pursued halal certification through the Malaysia Halal Corporation. 'Ayam' means 'chicken' in Indonesian and Malay. · Make a genuinely delicious Japanese ramen that observant Muslims and curious travelers alike can eat with peace of mind, by keeping the kitchen free of pork and alcohol and building flavor honestly from chicken rather than additives. · Tori-paitan (rich chicken) ramen served as the basic shoyu (soy) chicken soba and a richer shio (salt) chicken bowl, with miso also offered; the broths lean on chicken with a seafood aroma for depth, finished with finely minced onion and scallion, and m…
places.gfd: This is a standard ramen and tsukemen shop built on wheat noodles, with shoyu, shio and miso bowls whose tare typically contains wheat-based soy sauce. places.vgd: The house style is tori-paitan (rich chicken broth) and the signature bowls are chicken-based, so the standard menu is not vegan or vegetarian. The kitchen is halal (no pork, no alcohol) and avoids chemical seasonings, which makes it ingredient-conscious, but a plant-based diner would need to ask directly whether anything meat-free can be prepared and should not assume a vegan option exists.

places.chef: machi-chuka diner, local lunch and dinner spot · Nishikyogoku, Kyoto · A neighborhood machi-chuka (Japanese-style Chinese) restaurant that has fed the Nishikyogoku district for roughly 40 years, just east of Hankyu Nishikyogoku Station on Hanayacho-dori. It draws a cross-section of locals, from solo diners on their lunch break to families, in a bright, big-windowed room with a warm, unpretentious feel. · Honest, generous, affordable home-style Chinese cooking for the neighborhood — big portions, courteous service, and prices that keep regulars coming back day after day. · The signature bowl is the maabo-tenshinhan (mapo Tianjin rice): a fluffy egg over rice blanketed in a generous, glossy mapo sauce. The sauce is built on house-made fermented black bean paste (豆鼓醤) and several chili pastes with ginger and plenty of garlic, given depth by coarsely minced salted fermented black beans (豆鼓の粒) and finished with house chili oil, with finely minced pork for richness — kept addictively savory rather than punishingly hot, served around 1,050 yen with soup and pickles.

The signature mapo Tianjin rice rides on a mapo sauce that almost certainly contains wheat soy seasoning. There is no indication of gluten-free menus, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: No vegan offering. The kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward: pork features in the mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, and broths; dishes use animal-based stocks. Even otherwise plant-leaning items (fried rice, ankake) are cooked with meat/egg and shared woks. No vegetarian or vegan menu is advertised.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing
places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto (Nakagyo-ku, Gosho-minami / Karasuma-Oike area) · A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing — a cook with a reliable eye for ingredients who keeps the menu deliberately compact. · Keep the cooking simple and let quality ingredients carry it — the kind of place where, as one chef put it, everything you order somehow tastes good. Heat is balanced and aromatic rather than punishing. · Sichuan-style cooking pitched a notch upscale rather than fiery for its own sake: a fragrant tantanmen (the lunchtime dry 汁なし version is especially praised), a mapo tofu where the Sichuan pepper and chili oil are rounded out by the sweetness of the ground pork, plus boiled dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork.
places.gfd: A Sichuan Chinese kitchen built around wheat. The tantanmen and dumpling skins are wheat-flour, the chili/sesame tare and seasonings used in dishes like the mapo tofu lean on soy-based and bean-paste condiments that typically contain wheat, and there is no gluten-free menu or protocol. Not suitable for celiacs. A coeliac diner could ask whether any single rice- or vegetable-based plate could be prepared plainly, but cross-contact in a one-cook wok kitchen is unavoidable — treat as not GF-safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan specialist. The signature bowls (tantanmen, mapo tofu, boiled dumplings, sweet-and-sour pork) all use pork and/or animal-derived broth and condiments. places.chef: owner · 大阪（人類みな麺類系列） · Ramen Daisenso ("Ramen World War") is the Kyoto outpost of the acclaimed Osaka ramen group behind Jinrui Mina Menrui, the much-queued shop that turned shoyu ramen into something theatrical. places.chef: Kirameki Group (キラメキノ未来株式会社) operator · Kyoto, Japan · キラメキノ青空 is a Kyoto-grown ramen and mazesoba brand run by the Kirameki Group (キラメキノ未来株式会社), known across Kansai as one of the pioneers of Taiwan-style mazesoba. The owner leans into the romance of the form: an unmarked truck under a red lantern, a handful of spots, and a warm bowl eaten outdoors on a cold night. · The signature bowl is the 背脂チャッチャ (seabura chaccha) chuka soba — old-school Kyoto-style ramen: a pork-bone soy-sauce broth crowned with a generous shower of back fat, topped with chashu, with the salty-sharp snap of shoyu over slightly soft, chewy noodles (~780 yen). places.gfd: Not safe for celiac or strict gluten-free. This is a classic Kyoto-style chuka soba: wheat noodles in a pork-bone soy-sauce (shoyu) broth with back fat, and the shoyu tare almost certainly contains wheat. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodation is indicated, and as a single-operator truck-bed yatai there is no separate prep space. Avoid if you require gluten-free.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. All bowls are built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) soy broth with back fat and are topped with chashu (pork). No vegetable or vegan broth option is offered. There is nothing on the menu suitable for a strict vegan or vegetarian diner.
places.hours: ~19:00 to ~25:00 (1:00 the next day). Irregular days off. As a street stall, its operating days and location vary; the latest info is announced on Instagram.

places.n: 麺匠 一粒万倍 河原町店 (Menshou Ichiryu Manbai Kawaramachi-ten)

places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The signature bowl is extra-thick wheat noodles (blended with udon flour) dipped in a rich pork-bone-and-seafood broth, with a wheat-based shoyu/miso tare. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated prep, and as a busy mall food-court stall there is no allowance for managing cross-contamination. Avoid if you have celiac disease or a wheat allergy.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The core product is built on a pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) broth, topped with chashu pork and finished with animal-derived tare; menma and noodles are cooked in shared equipment. There is no vegan or vegetarian option advertised.

places.n: イワサキタンメン (Iwasaki Tanmen)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Iwasaki Tanmen opened its doors on March 1, 2023 in the Ono neighborhood of Yamashina, just steps from Ono Station, taking over a storefront that previously housed another ramen shop (Shioemon). places.chef: owner-operator · Ono, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto · Iwasaki Tanmen opened its doors on March 1, 2023 in the Ono neighborhood of Yamashina, just steps from Ono Station, taking over a storefront that previously housed another ramen shop (Shioemon). It is a rarity in Kyoto: a shop devoted to tanmen, a vegetable-piled salt ramen far more common in the Kanto region of eastern Japan than here in Kansai. · Make-it-your-own simplicity: diners can dial the vegetables, pork, noodle quantity, garlic and spice to taste, and garlic is served on the side so each guest controls their own portion. Sides like gyoza, karaage and takana rice round out an honest, affordable bowl. · The house tanmen is the signature: a mound of lightly stir-fried vegetables — cabbage, bean sprouts and more — over medium straight noodles in a chicken-and-pork salt (shio) broth. It arrives looking hearty and Jiro-esque, yet the soup is surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy back-fat. A pot of house chili-miso (kara-miso) sits at hand so you can stir in heat and depth gradually as you eat.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. Tanmen is built on wheat ramen noodles in a salt (shio) tare; the broth and house salt sauce are not documented as wheat-free, and there are no gluten-free noodle or accommodation options on the menu. No allergen handling is documented. Anyone with celiac disease or wheat allergy should treat this as unsafe.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The signature tanmen is a chicken-bone and pork-based salt broth topped with stir-fried pork and vegetables; pork and a chicken/pork stock are integral to every bowl. No plant-based broth or vegetable-only version is documented. A diner could potentially ask about a vegetable-heavy customization, but the base soup is animal-derived.
places.hours: Lunch 11:00-14:30, Dinner 18:00-22:00 (per Tabelog). One blog lists dinner as 18:00-21:00; treat evening close time as approximate. No regular closed day listed.

places.n: だし料理 十 (Dashi Ryori Jifu)

places.chef: Inoue (proprietor) · owner, chef · Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto — on the city's famous Ichijoji ramen street, but a deliberate step away from the heavy-broth pack. · The shop is the latest evolution of a Kyoto noodle maker who has spent years chasing dashi rather than richness. The lineage runs from a dashi-based ramen shop, Isao (イサオ, opened 2010), which the owner renamed and reframed in 2014 as Odashi to Komugi 130 (おだしと小麦 一三〇) to put the dashi and the wheat front and center. In June 2022 the concept was distilled again into だし料理 十. · The whole place is built so customers can actually understand dashi — you can watch it being made, taste it, and talk it through with the owner. Seasoning is pared back to almost nothing so the stock itself carries the bowl. · The signature bowl is the breakfast-only o-dashi no new-men: a clear soup built from just three things — Rishiri kombu, sawara (young Spanish mackerel / sagoshi), and bonito flakes — seasoned with a single gram of Iwate salt and no soy sauce at all. The noodles are made in-house from domestic wheat and egg, cut to roughly 1mm square and dusted with Hokkaido corn flour, then finished with hand-shaved bonito and a few pieces of sa…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature bowl centers on house-made noodles cut from domestic wheat and egg, so the core dish contains gluten. The broth itself is a clean fish dashi (Rishiri kombu, sawara/sagoshi, bonito) seasoned with salt only and no soy sauce, which removes one common wheat source — but the wheat noodle makes this unsafe for celiacs. No dedicated gluten-free preparation is advertised; a celiac diner would need to ask directly and likely cannot be accommodated.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian. The dashi is entirely animal-based (sawara/Spanish mackerel, bonito flakes, plus kombu), and the noodles contain egg. There is no plant-based bowl on offer.
places.hours: Wed–Thu, Sun 09:00–15:00; Fri–Sat 11:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:00); Mon–Tue closed. From around 16:00 the space shifts to a dashi retail shop / sake bar on the late-evening days.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kyoto Kitayama Motomachi Ramen traces its roots to a street cart (yatai) that the first-generation owner — a native of Kanazawa — set up on Shinmachi-dori in Kyoto's Kitayama district roughly 50 years ago. places.chef: owner, founder · Kyoto (Kitayama district yatai origins); founder from Kanazawa · Kyoto Kitayama Motomachi Ramen traces its roots to a street cart (yatai) that the first-generation owner — a native of Kanazawa — set up on Shinmachi-dori in Kyoto's Kitayama district roughly 50 years ago. Drawing on the rich, dark soy-sauce style of nearby Toyama Black, he built a Kyoto take on the bowl using tamari soy sauce from a long-established local soy-sauce maker. The business later moved into a permanent shop, settling at its current location in an alley off Higashinotoin in central Kyoto, where the cart's original flavor is carried on by a later (third) generation. · Honor the original yatai flavor while continuing to refine it; serve until the broth is gone and then close for the day. · A rich black-soy-sauce ramen finished with plenty of back fat (背脂醤油らーめん), with beef-tendon ramen (牛すじらーめん) as a second signature. The defining element is a specialty tamari soy sauce of the kind used for eel sauce, sourced from a 160-year-old Kyoto soy-sauce maker.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free and not celiac-safe. The ramen uses wheat noodles, a wheat-based tamari/black soy sauce tare (sourced from a long-established Kyoto soy sauce maker), and pork/beef broth. places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian options. The broth is a rich black soy sauce ramen built on pork/beef bases (beef tendon is a signature), the noodles are wheat, and the tare uses wheat-containing tamari soy sauce. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.

places.n: Bakery House Creek (ベーカリーハウス クリーク)
places.notes: [GF] Ask staff directly for the 米粉100％ (100% rice flour) items — the gluten-free 食パン (loaf), rice-flour bagels, cookies and cheesecake. Buy sealed/whole items rather than open-shelf loose bread to reduce cross-contact, and go early as the GF line sells out.

places.chef: Nobuo Kakine (垣根信夫) · Owner, Head pastry chef (シェフパティシエ) · Kyoto, Japan · OUBON opened in December 2017 a few minutes' walk from Fushimi Inari station in Fukakusa, Fushimi-ku. Head pastry chef and owner Nobuo Kakine (垣根信夫) is described as a veteran patissier with 40 years of experience in Kyoto, having served as head pâtissier at a well-known hotel and other shops before opening his own. The shop is credited as being run by a pâtissier who helped pioneer Japanese-style (和風) sweets. For its gluten-free line OUBON sources rice flour from Asahi Seifunjo (朝日製粉所) in the Kyoto Tamba/Nantan area. · To make rice-flour cakes so close to wheat versions that they are hard to tell apart in a blind test, so that people with wheat allergies can enjoy ordinary-tasting Western sweets alongside everyone else. · Rice-flour (米粉) gluten-free cakes and baked sweets — signature 豆乳米粉ロール, plus financiers and madeleines — alongside a conventional wheat pâtisserie range.
places.gfd: OUBON is a conventional Western pâtisserie near Fushimi Inari that sells regular wheat cakes AND a separate allergy-oriented 米粉 (rice-flour) line, so wheat is handled in the same kitchen. The shop's own claim for the rice-flour line reads: 「全てに米粉を使用していますのでアレルギーをお持ちの方でも、もちろん食べていただけます」 ("Everything uses rice flour, so even those with allergies can of course eat it"). Because the same bakery also produces wheat pastries daily, cross-contact with gluten is a real risk and this cannot be treated as …
places.vgd: The rice-flour items are not vegan: the shop lists 卵 (egg) and 乳 (dairy) as allergens on its gluten-free products. The signature 豆乳米粉ロール is described as 「グルテンフリー商品となっており、アレルギー物質は卵、乳」 and uses Hokkaido cream (whipped with soymilk), so egg and dairy remain. No vegan line is advertised.
places.hours: 10:00–20:00, closed Wednesdays (some listings show Wed 12:00–18:00). Tel 075-632-8287.

places.n: 土佐屋 室戸 (Tosaya Muroto)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop — a Tosa master, ~50 years at the counter] A tiny Kōchi (Tosa) izakaya on Kiyamachi just south of Sanjo — up on the 2nd floor above an Italian restaurant, with a ~10-seat counter plus one small tatami (6–8). The chef, a Tosa native with roughly half a century behind the grill, cooks yakitori over Tosa binchōtan charcoal and serves Kōchi's signature seared bonito (katsuo tataki), shamo (game-fowl) hot pot, and seasonal Tosa dishes. Reviewers praise thick, odorless bonito and carefully grilled skewers, and a charming old-Kyoto exterior; it draws locals and food-loving visitors alike. Reservations accepted (HotPepper). Address: 河原町通三条下ル大黒町49 (entrance on Kiyamachi-dōri). Instagram @tosayamuroto.
places.chef: master chef / owner (taishō) · Tosa (Kōchi Prefecture); the shop is in Kiyamachi, Nakagyo Ward, Kyoto · A Tosa (Kōchi) native who by most accounts has spent roughly fifty years cooking, running a small counter izakaya devoted to the food of his home region. He grills over Tosa binchōtan (the prized white charcoal of Kōchi) and centers the menu on Kōchi's most famous dish, seared bonito — the kind of veteran, single-counter kitchen where the chef works in front of you and the seasons drive what's served. · Charcoal yakitori over Tosa binchōtan and Kōchi's signature katsuo (bonito) tataki, plus shamo (game-fowl) hot pot and seasonal Tosa dishes.
places.gfd: A Tosa (Kōchi) izakaya built on charcoal yakitori and seared bonito (katsuo tataki) — soy sauce, yakitori tare and ponzu (all typically wheat-based) run through the menu, so it is not celiac-safe by default. Some items can be gluten-free if confirmed: sashimi, salt (shio) skewers, and salt-style katsuo tataki without ponzu. But the shared charcoal grill, shared fryer and wheat-containing sauces make cross-contamination likely — order shio, skip the tare/ponzu, and show the celiac card.
places.vgd: A Tosa seafood-and-yakitori counter: seared bonito, charcoal chicken, and shamo (game-fowl) hot pot. Bonito dashi and fish run through almost everything, so even vegetable dishes likely carry animal-derived stock. A few plain vegetable skewers or pickles may be possible, but confirm dashi/bonito with the chef. Not a vegan destination.
places.hours: Mon–Sat 17:00–23:00. Closed Sunday. (Some listings also note the 2nd & 3rd Monday closed and lunch by reservation only — confirm before visiting.)

places.hood: Oshibori-chō, Nakagyō-ku (NE corner of Horikawa-Oike, opposite Nijō Castle; 3 min from Ni…
places.notes: [Ramen · Fukuchiyama chain] The Kyoto-city branch of ふくちあん, a ramen company from Fukuchiyama in northern Kyoto Prefecture, on the northeast corner of the Horikawa-Oike crossing, across the road from Nijō Castle; it opened in 2022. The house bowl is a pork-bone and Tamba chicken-frame soup simmered for 20+ hours, seasoned with a brewed soy tare aged a year in cedar barrels, over thin house-made noodles, and comes with two kinds of pork, a seasoned egg and green onion. Kara-age is the other draw — the shop advertises a Karaage Grand Prix gold award. You buy a ticket at the machine; an English menu is posted outside and many of the customers are overseas visitors. The shop also advertises a miso-based vegetarian ramen.
places.chef: ramen company (株式会社新福知庵), Fukuchiyama · Fukuchiyama, northern Kyoto Prefecture — the chain's main shop is by JR Fukuchiyama Station · Fukuchian began as a change of trade: in 1996 a Fukuchiyama textile firm turned itself into a ramen business and opened the first ふくちあん. The company has since added branches in Kaibara, Kitaōji (Kyoto), Nijō-jō-mae (2022) and Shiga. · The founding-spirit essay on the company site: no textbook, soup after soup poured away, and the temptation to make life easier with ready-made soy tare and stock — refused, because "I don't want to tell a lie" (ウソは嫌なんです). · Ramen in a pork-bone and Tamba chicken soup with a year-aged brewed soy tare and house-made thin noodles; tender kara-age.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The chain's own allergen chart lists wheat (小麦) in every ramen, set, side and topping on it — including the chashu, seasoned egg and menma — and the noodles are made in-house from wheat flour. The shop says it cooks with ordinary shared utensils and dishes and leaves cross-contamination to the diner's own judgment. The only food item the chart shows without wheat is the sherbet. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: The regular bowls are built on a pork-bone and chicken-frame soup and topped with pork; the allergen chart lists pork and chicken for all of them. The shop does advertise a 'vegetarian ramen' (miso-based broth, house-made noodles), but in its own words it is made with 'almost no' (ほぼ) meat or fish ingredients — so do not assume it is vegan. Ask what the remaining animal ingredients are before ord…
